Week 0 (self-paced).title: Foundational Material & Pre-Program Foundations (self-paced orientation)
Week 0 (self-paced).content:
SWE Module 0 — Foundational Material & Pre-Program Foundations (self-paced orientation)

This layer is prerequisite scaffolding, not a live class, so it gets a short note rather than a full brief.

What it covers: Python essentials (data types, structures, conditionals, functions, Pandas) and an optional "Hello Agent" mini-project — a CSV FAQ agent built in Streamlit that lets a support user ask questions of a dataframe through an LLM plus a system prompt.

Why it matters: This mini-project introduces the core workflow used throughout the program—business requirement → prompt → model → tool → response.

Week 1.title: Agentic AI Foundations & Reflex Agents
Week 1.content:
SWE Module 1 — Agentic AI Foundations & Reflex Agents

1. Course Journey This is the atom of the entire program: a single agent that thinks, acts, and observes in a loop. It exists because everything later — RAG, multi-agent systems, MCP, fine-tuning — is an elaboration of this one primitive, and none of it makes sense until learners can see an LLM stop being a text box and start being a decision-maker. It sits first because the ReAct loop is the mental model every future module reuses. Each capstone system is, at its core, one or more of these agents wired together.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  Module 0 — Python essentials (self-paced): variables, data types, operators and strings; lists, tuples, sets and dictionaries; if-else, loops and functions; modules and packages.
•  Module 0 — Pandas basics: why Pandas, its core data structures, and filtering a DataFrame — enough to load, inspect and slice the data an agent's tools will return.
•  Pre-class primers for today: Prompting, Introduction to Agents, and LLM client libraries. Assume these were skimmed, not mastered — learners who skipped the optional mini-project may be making their first LLM API call today.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W0 Optional Mini-Project — Hello Agent (CSV FAQ Agent): a small Streamlit internal tool for support, product and operations staff: users upload CSV files and ask questions, an LLM plus a DataFrame agent answers from the data, and a system prompt controls the model's behavior. The real lesson was translating a business requirement into technical steps; its solution walkthrough is part of this week's topic list.
     Callback: ask which part of the app decided what to do next — nothing did. That missing decision step is today's agent loop. The project was optional, so expect a mixed room: demo it rather than assume it.

3. What learners will learn today By the end, learners can: explain what generative models and LLMs actually do and where they fail; write prompts deliberately rather than by trial and error; distinguish a fixed workflow from an autonomous agent; describe the Think–Act–Observe loop and trace it through a running agent; give an agent tools and short/long-term memory; and reason about when a single reflex agent is enough versus when a problem needs planning. They leave able to build a working tool-using agent, evidenced by the IT Support Agent assignment and the CRM Lead Qualifier project.

4. What this prepares learners for The agent loop is the spine of the course. Today's ReAct reasoning becomes the retrieval-augmented agent in RAG (W2–W3), the node behavior inside LangGraph (W4), the thing that gets voice and human checkpoints in W5, the client that calls MCP tools (W6), and the unit that gets traced and guardrailed in W8. Tool-calling introduced here is the exact mechanism MCP later standardizes.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  When you show the agent loop, remind them the Week 0 FAQ agent answered questions but couldn't choose an action — that gap is what today closes.
•  When you explain LLM limitations and hallucination, tell them this is precisely the motivation for RAG in two weeks — "we're about to give the agent a memory it can trust."
•  When you introduce tools, mention that in Week 6 these same tool calls get a universal protocol (MCP) so any agent can use any tool.
•  When you mention memory (short vs long term), foreshadow that long-term memory is what vector databases (W2) actually store.
•  When you touch on multi-agent systems as "the future," tell them Week 4 makes that future concrete with LangGraph.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How is an agent different from just prompting ChatGPT well?"
•  "If the LLM hallucinates, why would I trust an agent built on it?"
•  "When do I actually need an agent instead of a plain script with if-statements?"
•  "What's the difference between a workflow and an autonomous agent — isn't a loop just a workflow?"
•  "Do I have to use LangChain, or can I write the loop myself?"
•  "How does the agent 'know' which tool to call?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  An agent is a loop, not a single call — Think, Act, Observe, repeat.
2.  Tools are how an LLM touches the real world; without them it can only talk.
3.  LLM limitations (especially hallucination) are features of the terrain, not bugs to be prompted away — they motivate everything downstream.
4.  Autonomy is a spectrum; more autonomy means more need for the guardrails and evaluation coming later.
5.  Prompt engineering is necessary but not sufficient — it's the first tool, not the last.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "A good enough prompt removes the need for tools/RAG." Clarify that prompting shapes behavior but cannot inject knowledge the model doesn't have or verify facts — that's why the next four weeks exist.
•  "Agent = LangChain." Clarify that the agent loop is a concept; LangChain is one convenient implementation. They could build it with raw API calls.
•  "More autonomy is always better." Clarify that autonomy trades reliability for flexibility — a theme they'll feel acutely in Week 8.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Your learners arrive knowing Python and how to call an LLM, and maybe having built the Week 0 FAQ agent. Today they cross the line from "prompting a model" to "building an agent" — a reasoning loop that uses tools, keeps memory, and decides its own next step. That's the single most important conceptual jump in the program; protect time for the Think–Act–Observe loop and don't let prompt-engineering tangents eat it. Make sure they leave feeling the limitation that hallucination imposes, because next week you exploit exactly that pain to motivate retrieval. Everything from RAG to multi-agent systems to MCP is this same agent, extended. If they own the loop today, the rest of the course is elaboration; if they don't, every later module will feel like magic instead of engineering.

Week 2.title: RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents 1 (Retrieval Foundations)
Week 2.content:
SWE Module 2 — RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents 1 (Retrieval Foundations)

1. Course Journey Last week's agent could reason but only knew what was in its prompt and its training data. This module solves the knowledge problem: how does an agent retrieve the right information from a large private corpus by meaning rather than keyword? It appears now because retrieval is the first real answer to the hallucination pain learners felt in Week 1, and because every serious capstone needs grounded, source-backed answers. This is the "give the agent a reliable memory" week.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1 — LLMs and prompting: what Gen AI and LLMs are and where they are used, calling models through client libraries, deliberate prompt engineering, and the limitations of LLMs — hallucination above all.
•  W1 — The agent loop: workflows vs autonomous agents; Think–Act–Observe and the ReAct loop; the anatomy of an agent and the three pillars of agency; extending agents with tools; short- vs long-term memory; planning and reasoning; agentic design patterns.
•  W1 — Post-class reading: LLM limitations → RAG motivation, LLM hallucinations, a bird's-eye view of Transformers, LangChain, and OpenAI function calling — the RAG-motivation piece sets up today directly.
•  The gap they feel: a fixed prompt cannot scale to a large private knowledge base — their agents only know what fits in the prompt or the model's training data.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W1 Assignment — Autonomous IT Support Agent: a Level 1 IT support agent built with the OpenAI API (learners completed the ### TODO sections) that investigates server issues, checks server health and logs, restarts services automatically when CPU usage exceeds 90%, and escalates complex incidents to a human engineer.
     Callback: ask how it would find the fix for an error that isn't in its prompt — searching a runbook by meaning is today's problem.
•  W1 Project — Autonomous CRM Lead Qualifier Agent: given a lead's email address, the agent extracts the company domain, gathers industry, size and revenue, checks internal CRM records for past interactions, assigns a High/Medium/Low priority and writes a concise summary for the sales rep.
     Callback: ask what changes if the CRM history is thousands of free-text call notes — that is a retrieval problem, not a prompting problem.
•  W0 Hello Agent (optional): the CSV FAQ agent in Streamlit — their first pass at the business requirement → prompt → model → tool → response workflow.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain why semantic retrieval beats keyword search; turn text into embeddings and reason about similarity; choose and apply chunking strategies (fixed, semantic, recursive, structure-based, LLM-based); store and query vectors in a vector database (Chroma); and pick among indexing strategies (vector, summary, tree, keyword, hybrid) for different query types. They leave able to build the retrieval half of a RAG system, evidenced by the SupportDesk-RAG Part 1 project.

4. What this prepares learners for Retrieval built here becomes the R in the full RAG pipeline of W3, the knowledge tool an agent calls in multi-agent systems (W4), and the thing whose quality gets seriously upgraded in Hybrid Search (W7) with sparse/dense vectors and RRF. Chunking and indexing choices made today resurface as tuning knobs in evaluation (W8) and as a core "RAG vs fine-tuning" decision in W9.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Open by reminding them: last week the agent hallucinated because it had no trustworthy source — embeddings are how we build that source.
•  When you introduce vector databases, stress this is the long-term memory you gestured at in Week 1's memory discussion.
•  When you compare chunking strategies, tell them chunk quality directly caps retrieval quality — which they'll measure with real metrics in Week 3 and optimize again in Week 7.
•  When you show indexing strategies, foreshadow that Week 7's hybrid search exists because pure semantic vectors miss exact-match terms.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "What's the difference between an embedding and a vector database?"
•  "How do I choose a chunk size — is there a right answer?"
•  "Does RAG replace fine-tuning? When would I do one over the other?"
•  "Why not just stuff the whole document into the context window?"
•  "How do I know if my retrieval is actually good?"
•  "Which vector database should I use in production?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Embeddings are numerical meaning; retrieval is nearest-neighbor search over that meaning.
2.  Chunking is a design decision that silently determines answer quality.
3.  A vector database is infrastructure for storing and searching embeddings — it is not the embedding.
4.  Retrieval is a component you can measure and improve, not a black box.
5.  RAG grounds answers in sources; it is the primary defense against hallucination.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Embeddings and vector databases are the same thing." Clarify: embeddings are numerical representations of meaning; vector databases store and retrieve them efficiently. This is the single most common confusion at this stage.
•  "Bigger context windows make RAG obsolete." Clarify that cost, latency, and the "lost in the middle" problem keep retrieval essential even with huge windows.
•  "RAG and fine-tuning are competitors." Clarify they solve different problems (knowledge vs behavior) — a distinction Week 9 makes precise.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners come in having felt hallucination as a real limitation last week. Today they get the standard industry answer: retrieve grounded knowledge by semantic similarity. The three ideas that must land are that embeddings encode meaning, that a vector database is just efficient storage-and-search for those embeddings, and that chunking quietly governs everything downstream. Keep the embeddings-vs-vector-DB distinction crisp — it's the misconception that follows learners for weeks. They leave able to retrieve; next week they wrap retrieval into a full pipeline with generation and, crucially, evaluation. Frame today as building the memory, and Week 3 as learning whether the memory is any good.

Week 3.title: RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents 2 (Pipeline, Evaluation & Agentic RAG)
Week 3.content:
SWE Module 3 — RAG-Powered Knowledge Agents 2 (Pipeline, Evaluation & Agentic RAG)

1. Course Journey Week 2 built retrieval; this week turns it into a complete, measurable, and agentic system. It exists because a retrieval demo that works on three documents is not a production RAG system — learners need the full pipeline (indexing + querying), evaluation metrics, and the ability to let an agent decide when and how to retrieve. It sits here because you cannot improve what you cannot measure, and evaluation discipline introduced now pays off in every later module. This is where RAG graduates from "cool demo" to "engineering."

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W2 — Semantic retrieval: the three critical gaps that motivate semantic retrieval; text embeddings and similarity scoring; storing and querying embeddings in a vector store (post-class: an embeddings + Pinecone notebook and access control for vector databases).
•  W2 — Chunking strategies: fixed-size, semantic, recursive, document-structure-based and LLM-based chunking — and the idea that chunk quality caps retrieval quality.
•  W2 — Indexing and routing: why production RAG keeps multiple indexes (vector, summary, tree, keyword, hybrid), intent-based query routing, and the core retrieval loop "in one picture."
•  W1 — Agents and tool-calling: the ReAct loop, tools and memory — the machinery today's Agentic RAG reuses.
•  The gap they feel: they can retrieve, but have no way yet to quantify whether retrieval — or the final answer — is any good.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W2 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 1: on support-ticket data, learners generated embeddings and implemented semantic search, chunked documents, built Chroma vector stores, and compared Vector, Summary, Tree, Keyword and Hybrid indexes.
     Callback: this week's SupportDesk-RAG Part 2 adds generation, evaluation and an agent on top of this exact retrieval layer — have them keep it open.
•  W2 Assignment — Retrieval exercises: three hands-on exercises: semantic search (embeddings, similarity scores, filtering), chunking plus vector-database storage, search and filtering at scale, and a trade-off comparison of Vector, Summary, Tree and Keyword indexes.
•  W1 builds: the Autonomous IT Support Agent (assignment) and the CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (project) — their first tool-using agents.
     Callback: the tool-calling loop from these builds returns today as an agent deciding whether to retrieve.
•  Earlier builds: Hello Agent CSV FAQ agent (W0, optional).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: assemble a complete RAG pipeline (offline indexing + online querying) with citations, fallback handling, metadata filtering, and conversational memory; evaluate retrieval with Precision/Recall/F1 and generation with groundedness and completeness; and build Agentic RAG with LangChain, where the agent itself decides whether, what, and how many times to retrieve. They leave able to ship and defend a RAG system, evidenced by SupportDesk-RAG Part 2.

4. What this prepares learners for The evaluation habits formed here become the backbone of W8 (Observability, Evaluation & Safety) and the LangSmith evaluation step in W9 fine-tuning. Agentic RAG — an agent choosing its retrieval strategy — is the conceptual bridge to multi-agent systems (W4), where routing decisions become explicit. The pipeline structure recurs in the capstone and in the Agentic Research and Text-to-SQL interview deep dives.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Remind them Week 2 gave them retrieval but no way to know if it was good — today's metrics are that missing feedback loop.
•  When you teach groundedness, connect it straight back to Week 1's hallucination problem: "this metric literally measures how much the model made up."
•  When you introduce Agentic RAG, note that letting the agent decide to retrieve is a preview of the routing logic in next week's multi-agent systems.
•  When you cover retrieval metrics, tell them Week 7's hybrid search is one concrete way to move these numbers.
•  Point out that today's evaluation mindset is the same one they'll apply to whole agent systems in Week 8.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "What counts as 'good' Precision or Recall for RAG — is there a benchmark?"
•  "How is Agentic RAG different from just always retrieving?"
•  "If my groundedness is low, is it a retrieval problem or a generation problem?"
•  "Do I need conversational memory for every RAG app?"
•  "Isn't LLM-as-a-judge circular — using an LLM to grade an LLM?"
•  "When does RAG stop being enough and I need multiple agents?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  RAG is a two-phase pipeline: offline indexing and online querying — most bugs live at the seam.
2.  You cannot improve retrieval you don't measure; metrics are non-negotiable, not academic.
3.  Groundedness is the direct, quantified answer to hallucination.
4.  Agentic RAG means the agent decides its retrieval strategy — reasoning applied to knowledge.
5.  Low answer quality has two possible root causes (retrieval vs generation); diagnosis matters more than a single score.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "High retrieval recall means good answers." Clarify that generation can still fabricate from correct context — retrieval and generation quality are separate axes.
•  "Agentic RAG is just RAG with extra steps." Clarify that the agent's ability to skip, repeat, or reformulate retrieval is a genuine capability jump, not decoration.
•  "Evaluation is a final polish step." Clarify that without evaluation, every improvement afterward is guesswork — this is why it comes now, not at the end.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive able to retrieve but blind to whether their retrieval is any good. Today closes that loop: the full pipeline, real metrics (Precision/Recall/F1, groundedness, completeness), and Agentic RAG where the agent chooses its own retrieval path. The mindset shift — measure, then improve — is the real deliverable and it recurs in Weeks 8 and 9. Make sure they leave able to diagnose whether a bad answer is a retrieval failure or a generation failure, because that diagnostic skill is what separates people who tune RAG from people who guess. Next week the "agent deciding what to do" idea scales up: instead of one agent choosing retrieval, many agents coordinate.

Week 4.title: Multi-Agent Systems (LangGraph)
Week 4.content:
SWE Module 4 — Multi-Agent Systems (LangGraph)

1. Course Journey Until now every problem was solved by one agent. This module exists because real systems decompose work across specialized agents — a researcher, a writer, a router — coordinated by explicit state. It appears here because learners have now seen a single agent make routing decisions (Agentic RAG), and the natural next question is "what if the decision is which agent handles this?" LangGraph gives them the graph-and-state machinery to answer that. This is the week the course stops being about agents and starts being about architectures.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W3 — Full RAG pipeline: offline indexing plus online querying, the LangChain component stack, conversation with history, and production touches — citations, fallbacks and metadata filtering.
•  W3 — RAG evaluation: the two-layer framework, ground-truth setup, Precision@K / Recall@K / F1@K and K trade-offs, groundedness and completeness, LLM-as-judge, targets and alert thresholds, a failure-pattern playbook, and A/B testing.
•  W3 — Agentic RAG with LangChain: direct vs agentic RAG, tool design principles and multi-step reasoning — an agent deciding whether, what and how often to retrieve. This is the routing decision today scales up.
•  W2 — Retrieval foundations: embeddings, chunking strategies, Chroma, indexing strategies and intent-based query routing.
•  W1 — The agent loop: ReAct, tools, and short- vs long-term memory — every node they build today is one of these agents.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: a production-style RAG system: ingestion, embeddings in a vector store, retrieval, and grounded generation with prompt-engineering and validation guards against hallucination — evaluated on Precision/Recall/F1 plus groundedness/completeness, then finished as Agentic RAG with dynamic tool selection, multi-step reasoning and conversational context.
     Callback: their agent already chose between tools; today it chooses between agents.
•  W3 Assignment — RAG support assistant: the full pipeline with prompt engineering, retrieval optimization, citation handling, fallback mechanisms, metadata filtering and conversational memory; evaluated on retrieval and generation metrics; extended into Agentic RAG with custom tools, improved tool selection, multi-step reasoning and robust error handling.
•  W3 Post-class (optional) — Financial Bot with LLMs: financial data embedded into Chroma through LangChain, served by a RAG pipeline in a Streamlit app deployed on Streamlit Cloud.
•  Earlier builds: SupportDesk-RAG Part 1 and the retrieval exercises (W2); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1); Hello Agent (W0, optional).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain why and when to split work across multiple agents; model an application as a LangGraph graph with explicit shared state; build specialized sub-agents and route between them; implement tool-calling loops inside nodes; and reason about orchestration patterns (supervisor/router, specialist agents). They leave able to design and build a coordinated multi-agent system, evidenced by the Travel Planning multi-agent project and the multi-agent content-writer assignment.

4. What this prepares learners for LangGraph state is the single most reused artifact from here on. It becomes the foundation for sub-graphs and Human-in-the-Loop (W5), the client side of MCP/A2A orchestration (W6), the thing you trace and evaluate in W8, and the backbone of the capstone and the advanced Multi-Agent Coordination deep dive (W14). If learners don't internalize state today, every later multi-agent topic wobbles.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the jump directly: "Last week one agent decided whether to retrieve; this week we decide which agent should act."
•  When you introduce LangGraph state, tell them explicitly: "hold onto this — Voice Agents, HITL, MCP orchestration, and your capstone all run on this same state object."
•  When you show specialist agents, remind them each specialist is just a Week 1 agent — nothing new inside the node, only new wiring between nodes.
•  When you discuss orchestration overhead, preview Week 8's cost and latency concerns — more agents means more calls to pay for and trace.
•  Mention that in Week 6 these agents will talk to external agents and tools through standard protocols.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Why can't one clever agent do everything instead of many agents?"
•  "Is LangGraph mandatory, or can I orchestrate agents myself?"
•  "What exactly is 'state' and why does it need to be explicit?"
•  "How do agents pass information to each other?"
•  "Doesn't adding agents just add cost and latency?"
•  "How is this different from just calling functions in sequence?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Multi-agent design is decomposition — split by responsibility, not for its own sake.
2.  Explicit shared state is what makes coordination reliable and debuggable.
3.  Each agent is still a Week-1 loop; the novelty is the graph that connects them.
4.  Orchestration has a cost — more agents means more latency, spend, and failure surface.
5.  A supervisor/router pattern is the workhorse; learn it before exotic topologies.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "More agents is automatically better/smarter." Clarify that every added agent adds coordination cost and new failure modes — decomposition must earn its keep.
•  "State is just conversation history." Clarify that LangGraph state is a structured, shared object the whole graph reads and writes — far more than a chat log.
•  "LangGraph is the only way." Clarify it's a powerful framework, but the underlying idea is a state machine over agents; the concept transfers.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive able to build one capable agent and to let it route its own retrieval. Today they scale that instinct outward: many specialized agents, coordinated through an explicit LangGraph state object. The key realization is that nothing inside a node is new — each node is still last month's agent — and that all the difficulty (and power) lives in the wiring and the shared state. Hammer the state concept, because Voice Agents, Human-in-the-Loop, MCP orchestration, the capstone, and the Week 14 deep dive all sit on top of it. Warn them early that more agents is not free: it buys flexibility with latency, cost, and debugging pain — which is exactly what Week 8 will teach them to manage.

Week 5.title: Multimodal Conversational System (Voice, Sub-Graphs, HITL)
Week 5.content:
SWE Module 5 — Multimodal Conversational System (Voice, Sub-Graphs, HITL)

1. Course Journey Learners can now coordinate agents, but everything so far has been text and fully autonomous. This module exists to add two things production systems demand: a voice/multimodal interface, and a human checkpoint for high-stakes actions. It sits here because both features are built on top of LangGraph state — you need last week's machinery before you can add sub-graphs and interrupts. This is the week agents become things a real person can talk to and safely supervise.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W4 — Multi-agent design: what multi-agent systems are, why and when to build them, the core principle, common workflows and agent patterns, the popular frameworks, and when to use — and not use — sub-agents (post-class reading: Multi-Agent Systems & Orchestration).
•  W4 — LangGraph core: graphs built from states and nodes, the explicit State object, persistence and the Memory Store; tool-calling loops inside nodes; checkpointers for memory across sessions.
•  W2–W3 — RAG as a callable tool: embeddings, Chroma, the full pipeline, evaluation metrics and Agentic RAG — today's menu and product search agents are RAG tools inside a graph.
•  W1 — The agent loop: every specialist is still a ReAct agent; voice and HITL wrap around it rather than change it.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W4 Project — Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System: specialist agents search flights and hotels, plan complete itineraries, answer travel questions with deep research and handle multiple queries in parallel, then present one unified, well-formatted recommendation.
     Callback: its coordinator-plus-specialists shape is the orchestrator they extend today with sub-graphs and a human checkpoint.
•  W4 Assignment — Multi-Agent Content Writer (LangGraph): a router sends each request to an SEO Blog Writer, an X/Twitter Writer or a General Handler; agents run tool-calling loops with research and internet-search tools; a checkpointer gives persistent, context-aware memory across sessions.
     Callback: that checkpointer is what makes today's interrupt-and-resume possible — HITL needs saved state to resume from.
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: an evaluated Agentic RAG system — the same retrieval pattern reappears today as the menu and product search tools.
•  Earlier builds: SupportDesk-RAG Part 1 (W2); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1); optional Financial Bot (W3) and Hello Agent (W0).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: build voice agents (speech-to-text → reasoning → text-to-speech) and reason about the audio stack; compose sub-graphs to modularize complex LangGraph applications; and implement Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) so an agent pauses for human approval or missing information before acting. They leave able to build a supervised, multi-modal conversational system, evidenced by the SnackStack multi-agent food-delivery assignment.

4. What this prepares learners for HITL is the conceptual seed of the guardrails and safety work in W8 and the autonomy/safety tradeoffs in the advanced deep dives (W14–W15). Sub-graphs are the modularization pattern learners will reach for in the capstone when a single flat graph becomes unmanageable. Voice and real-time interaction reappear as a design consideration in latency/cost discussions.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Point out that sub-graphs are just last week's graphs nested — "you already know how to build these; now we compose them."
•  When you introduce HITL, frame it as the first deliberate limit on autonomy — and tell them Week 8 turns this instinct into systematic guardrails.
•  When you cover voice latency, connect to the cost/latency themes coming in Week 8 and the LLMOps weeks.
•  Remind them the orchestrator routing to a Menu Agent vs an Order Agent is the same supervisor pattern from Week 4 — only now one branch waits for a human.
•  Note that a voice agent is still a Week-1 agent loop wearing an audio interface.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When should an agent stop and ask a human versus just act?"
•  "Do sub-graphs add real value or just complexity?"
•  "How much latency does voice add, and does it break the experience?"
•  "Is HITL the same as guardrails?"
•  "Can I add voice to any of my earlier agents?"
•  "How does the agent handle being interrupted mid-task?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Multimodality is an interface layer over the same agent loop — the reasoning doesn't change.
2.  Sub-graphs are modular composition; use them when one graph gets too big to reason about.
3.  HITL is intentional, designed non-autonomy at the points that matter.
4.  Human checkpoints are a reliability tool, not an admission of failure.
5.  Real-time interaction introduces latency budgets you must design around.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Voice agents are a fundamentally different kind of AI." Clarify they're the same reasoning loop with audio in/out bolted on.
•  "HITL means the agent is just doing what humans tell it." Clarify HITL is selective — the agent runs autonomously except at defined high-stakes checkpoints.
•  "Sub-graphs are advanced/optional." Clarify they're the standard way to keep complex systems maintainable, which the capstone will demand.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners come in able to orchestrate text agents through LangGraph state. Today they add the two things that make agents deployable to real users: a voice/multimodal interface and human-in-the-loop checkpoints. Emphasize that neither changes the agent's core reasoning — voice is an interface, HITL is a control point — both are built directly on last week's graph and state. The most valuable idea to leave them with is deliberate non-autonomy: choosing where a human must approve. That instinct becomes formal guardrails in Week 8 and mature autonomy tradeoffs in the final deep dives. Next week the agents stop being self-contained and start talking to the outside world — and to each other — through standard protocols.

Week 6.title: Agent Communication Protocols: MCP, A2A & Google ADK
Week 6.content:
SWE Module 6 — Agent Communication Protocols: MCP, A2A & Google ADK

1. Course Journey So far, tools were hand-wired into each agent and agents lived in one codebase. This module exists to standardize two things: how an agent connects to external tools and data (MCP), and how independent agents talk to each other (A2A), with Google ADK as a concrete framework. It appears now because learners have built multi-agent systems (W4) and supervised them (W5) — the next scaling problem is interoperability across systems and vendors. This is the week agents stop being islands.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1 — Tool-calling: tools as functions an agent chooses to call, plus OpenAI function calling (post-class reading). Every tool so far has been hand-wired into one agent's code — the friction MCP removes.
•  W4 — Multi-agent orchestration: LangGraph State, routing to specialists, persistence, checkpointers and the Memory Store, and when to use sub-agents.
•  W5 — Voice and sub-graphs: chained ("sandwich") vs speech-to-speech realtime voice architectures; composing sub-graphs — called inside a node or added as a node — with their own persistence.
•  W5 — Human-in-the-loop: pausing a graph with interrupts and resuming it once a human approves or supplies missing information.
•  W5 — Post-class reading: GenAI for Audio — text-to-speech, speaker diarization, WaveNet, voice with LLMs and vocoders.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W5 Project — AxiomCart (Multi-Agent Voice-Enabled Shopping Assistant): built in nine stages on LangGraph, LangChain and GPT-4o: foundation; a RAG product-search tool; a Product Agent sub-graph; a Support Agent with tools; an orchestrator with multi-agent routing; a synthesizer and full graph; human-in-the-loop; an interactive REPL; and voice I/O.
     Callback: every tool in AxiomCart lives inside that one codebase — ask what it would take to let another team's agent use its product search. That is the problem MCP solves.
•  W5 Assignment — SnackStack: a food-delivery assistant in which an LLM-powered orchestrator routes to a Menu Agent (RAG-based menu search over ChromaDB) and an Order Agent that tracks orders and asks a human for missing details — with structured outputs, checkpointer memory and optional voice.
     Callback: the Order Agent's human-in-the-loop step reappears in this week's exercises as HITL approvals inside ADK/A2A negotiations.
•  W4 builds: the Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System (project) and the Multi-Agent Content Writer (assignment) — their reference designs for routing and tool-calling loops.
•  Earlier builds: SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1); optional Financial Bot (W3) and Hello Agent (W0).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain what MCP standardizes and why (a universal interface between agents and tools/data); build and connect MCP servers, including multiple servers with automatic tool discovery and resilient error handling; implement agent-to-agent (A2A) communication and negotiation; and build multi-agent systems with Google ADK including governance callbacks. They leave able to build interoperable, protocol-based agent systems, evidenced by the MCP/ADK/A2A exercises and the Real Estate Negotiation project.

4. What this prepares learners for MCP is the production-standard way learners will connect tools in the capstone and beyond. The governance callbacks introduced here foreshadow guardrails (W8). A2A negotiation is a direct precursor to the Multi-Agent Coordination deep dive (W14), where agent contracts and failure modes get rigorous. Error-handling and self-correction patterns seen here recur in reliability discussions across the LLMOps weeks.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback: "In Week 1 you hand-wired tools into the agent. MCP is the industry's answer to doing that once, reusably, for any tool."
•  When you show multiple MCP servers with tool discovery, connect to Week 4 — "your orchestrator now discovers capabilities instead of hard-coding them."
•  When you cover A2A negotiation, tell them Week 14 turns this into formal agent roles, contracts, and coordination-failure analysis.
•  When governance callbacks appear, preview Week 8: "this is guardrails in miniature."
•  Remind them server failure recovery and LLM self-correction are the same reliability muscle they'll exercise in the LLMOps weeks.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When would I use MCP instead of just calling a function directly?"
•  "Is MCP replacing LangChain / tool-calling, or complementing it?"
•  "What's the difference between MCP (agent↔tools) and A2A (agent↔agent)?"
•  "Do I need Google ADK, or is it one option among many?"
•  "What happens when an MCP server goes down mid-request?"
•  "Why do agents need to 'negotiate' — can't they just share data?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  MCP standardizes the agent-to-tool boundary so tools become reusable across agents and vendors.
2.  A2A is a different axis — standardizing agent-to-agent interaction, including negotiation.
3.  Protocols exist to solve scaling and interoperability, not to add ceremony.
4.  Resilient error handling and self-correction are first-class design concerns, not afterthoughts.
5.  Governance callbacks are where safety starts entering the architecture.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "MCP replaces tool-calling / LangChain." Clarify MCP is a standard interface for tools; the agent still calls tools — MCP just makes them portable.
•  "MCP and A2A are the same idea." Clarify the axes: MCP connects agents to tools/data; A2A connects agents to agents.
•  "Protocols are enterprise overhead I can skip." Clarify that without them, every integration is bespoke and brittle — the pain scales with the system.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive able to build and supervise multi-agent systems inside a single codebase. Today they learn the protocols that let those systems reach outward: MCP for tools and data, A2A for agent-to-agent negotiation, with Google ADK as a working framework. The clarifying distinction to protect is the two axes — MCP (agent↔tools) versus A2A (agent↔agents) — because learners conflate them constantly. Frame protocols as the answer to scaling and interoperability, the natural sequel to last month's orchestration. Governance callbacks here are a quiet preview of Week 8 guardrails, and A2A negotiation is the seed of the Week 14 coordination deep dive. Next week the course pivots back to retrieval quality with hybrid search.

Week 7.title: Hybrid Search & Retrieval
Week 7.content:
SWE Module 7 — Hybrid Search & Retrieval

1. Course Journey Weeks 2–3 established semantic retrieval, but pure vector search has a blind spot: it misses exact terms, codes, and rare keywords. This module exists to fix retrieval quality by fusing semantic (dense) and lexical (sparse) search. It appears after learners have built and evaluated RAG, because only now do they have the metrics and the felt experience to appreciate why one retrieval method isn't enough. This is the "make retrieval production-grade" week, and it directly moves the numbers learners learned to measure in Week 3.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W2 — Dense retrieval: embeddings and similarity, chunking strategies, Chroma, and the five index types (vector, summary, tree, keyword, hybrid) — they have met a hybrid index but not built one from first principles.
•  W3 — Retrieval evaluation: Precision@K, Recall@K and F1@K, K trade-offs, ground-truth setup, groundedness and completeness, LLM-as-judge — the scoreboard today's hybrid search should move.
•  W4–W6 — Retrieval inside larger systems: RAG tools inside LangGraph agents (SnackStack's menu search, AxiomCart's product search) and, most recently, data served to agents through MCP servers.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W2 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 1: they already compared Vector, Summary, Tree, Keyword and Hybrid indexes on support-ticket data.
     Callback: ask whether exact identifiers — ticket IDs, error codes, product names — retrieved well with pure vector search. That failure is today's motivation for sparse vectors.
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: measured their pipeline with Precision/Recall/F1 and groundedness/completeness, and built Agentic RAG on top.
     Callback: those scores are the baseline; RRF is a lever to move them.
•  W6 Project — Real Estate Negotiation Workshop: autonomous Buyer and Seller agents negotiate property prices using real-time market and inventory data from MCP servers, orchestrated with Google ADK and communicating over A2A.
•  W6 Assignment — MCP, ADK and A2A exercises: extending MCP agents with new tools, integrating multiple servers with automatic tool discovery, server-failure recovery and LLM self-correction; then ADK/A2A systems with governance callbacks, negotiation-stall detection, hierarchical delegation, prompt-injection defenses, HITL approvals, parallel negotiations and shared memory.
•  Earlier builds: AxiomCart and SnackStack (W5); Travel Planner and Content Writer (W4); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1); optional Financial Bot (W3) and Hello Agent (W0).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: distinguish sparse (lexical, e.g. BM25) from dense (semantic) vectors and know when each wins; trace the evolution from keyword search to modern hybrid approaches; combine both retrieval methods and fuse their rankings with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF); and use tools like Qdrant to build a hybrid pipeline. They leave able to build and tune a hybrid retrieval system, evidenced by the PubMedQA biomedical hybrid-search project.

4. What this prepares learners for Hybrid search is a concrete lever for the retrieval quality that evaluation (W8) measures and the capstone depends on. The dense/sparse distinction and RRF reappear in the Agentic Research Systems and Text-to-SQL deep dives (W12–W13), where schema and document retrieval must be both precise and semantic. It also sharpens the RAG-vs-fine-tuning reasoning in W9 — sometimes better retrieval, not a new model, is the fix.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Open by returning to a Week 2/3 failure: "Remember when semantic search missed the exact product code? That's the gap sparse vectors fill."
•  When you teach RRF, tie it back to Week 3 metrics — "this is how we push Recall up without wrecking Precision."
•  Remind them dense retrieval is exactly the embeddings pipeline from Week 2; they're adding a second, complementary retriever, not replacing the first.
•  Connect to Week 9: "before you fine-tune to fix bad answers, check whether hybrid retrieval fixes them cheaper."
•  Note that hybrid retrieval will be a default assumption in the later system-design deep dives.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "If embeddings capture meaning, why do we still need keyword search?"
•  "What is RRF actually doing to combine the two rankings?"
•  "Is hybrid search always better, or does it depend on the data?"
•  "Won't running two retrievers double my latency and cost?"
•  "Does this replace the vector database from Week 2?"
•  "How do I decide the weighting between sparse and dense?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Dense and sparse retrieval have complementary strengths — meaning vs exact match.
2.  RRF is a simple, robust way to fuse rankings without tuning fragile weights.
3.  Hybrid search is a quality lever you reach for when metrics stall.
4.  Better retrieval is often a cheaper fix than a bigger model or fine-tuning.
5.  Every added retriever costs latency — quality gains must justify the spend.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Semantic search made keyword search obsolete." Clarify that exact terms, IDs, and rare tokens are where lexical search still wins — hence hybrid.
•  "Hybrid search is a different system from RAG." Clarify it's an upgrade to the retrieval step inside RAG, not a replacement for it.
•  "RRF needs heavy tuning." Clarify RRF's appeal is that it works well with minimal configuration compared to weighted score fusion.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive having built RAG and, crucially, having measured it — so they know retrieval quality is finite and improvable. Today gives them the strongest single retrieval upgrade in the course: fuse semantic and lexical search with RRF. Anchor the whole session in a concrete Week-2 failure (a missed exact term) so the motivation is visceral, then show how hybrid retrieval moves the exact Precision/Recall numbers they learned in Week 3. The takeaway to leave them with is strategic, not just technical: better retrieval is frequently the cheapest fix — worth checking before reaching for fine-tuning in Week 9. Next week the focus shifts from building capability to making whole systems observable, safe, and affordable.

Week 8.title: Agent Observability, Evaluation & Safety
Week 8.content:
SWE Module 8 — Agent Observability, Evaluation & Safety

1. Course Journey Learners can now build capable, interoperable, multimodal agent systems — but "it works on my demo" is not "it's safe and affordable in production." This module exists to make systems trustworthy: traceable, measurable, guarded, and cost-controlled. It sits here, right before the production/ops weeks, because it converts the ad-hoc evaluation habits from Week 3 into a systematic discipline applied to entire agent systems. This is the week engineering rigor becomes non-negotiable.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W3 — The evaluation mindset: two-layer (retrieval + generation) evaluation, Precision/Recall/F1@K, groundedness and completeness, LLM-as-judge, alert thresholds, a failure-pattern playbook and A/B testing — "measure, then improve."
•  W4–W6 — Systems too complex to debug by eye: LangGraph multi-agent graphs with routing, sub-graphs, checkpointers and interrupts; MCP tool loops across multiple servers; ADK/A2A agents exchanging messages.
•  W5–W6 — Early safety controls: HITL interrupts for high-stakes steps; ADK governance callbacks, prompt-injection defenses and negotiation-stall detection.
•  W7 — Retrieval-quality levers: dense vs sparse vectors, k-NN, ANN and HNSW, inverted indexes and SPLADE, and hybrid search fused with RRF in Qdrant (with FastEmbed).
Projects and assignments already built
•  W7 Project — Hybrid Search & Retrieval System (PubMedQA): loaded and cleaned biomedical abstracts, built searchable text from structured fields, generated dense and sparse embeddings, indexed both in Qdrant, queried the two indexes in parallel, fused results with RRF, and compared dense-only, sparse-only and hybrid retrieval.
     Callback: that three-way comparison was an evaluation — today generalizes it to whole agent systems with LangSmith and DeepEval.
•  W6 Project — Real Estate Negotiation Workshop: Buyer and Seller agents on MCP market data, orchestrated in ADK and talking over A2A.
     Callback: ask how they debugged a stalled negotiation or a wrong turn — that pain is today's "silent failure problem."
•  W6 Assignment — MCP, ADK and A2A exercises: included governance callbacks, prompt-injection defenses and HITL approvals.
     Callback: ask which of those defenses they would keep in production — today's four-strategy guardrail pipeline answers that systematically.
•  W5 builds — AxiomCart and SnackStack: multi-agent, voice-capable systems with orchestrators, RAG tools and HITL.
     Callback: good live examples of "every query = 2+ LLM calls" when you reach cost.
•  Earlier builds: Travel Planner and Content Writer (W4); SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1); optional Financial Bot (W3) and Hello Agent (W0).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: instrument agents for observability (trace and debug multi-step behavior with LangSmith); build evaluation frameworks (custom metrics, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge with DeepEval); implement layered guardrails on inputs and outputs (regex, moderation APIs, Presidio, Guardrails AI, LLM-based checks); and measure and reduce cost. They leave able to operate an agent system responsibly, evidenced by the multi-agent FinTech support project.

4. What this prepares learners for This is the direct foundation for LLMOps Part 1 & 2 (W8a, W9a) and the LangSmith evaluation step in fine-tuning (W9). Observability and eval are assumed baseline skills in the capstone and are the entire subject of the Self-Improving Agents deep dive (W15). Cost optimization reasoning recurs in every "which model / how big a GPU" decision later.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback: "In Week 3 you evaluated retrieval; today you evaluate the whole agent system — same mindset, bigger scope."
•  When you show tracing, remind them how painful debugging felt in Week 4's multi-agent project — tracing is the cure.
•  When you teach guardrails, connect to Week 5 HITL and Week 6 governance callbacks: "those were early instincts; this is the systematic version."
•  When you cover cost, tie it back to Week 4's warning that more agents means more spend — now they can measure it.
•  Preview that Week 15's entire deep dive is about agents evaluating and improving themselves using exactly these tools.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Isn't using an LLM to judge an LLM (LLM-as-judge) circular?"
•  "How many guardrails is enough — where do I stop?"
•  "What's the difference between observability and evaluation?"
•  "How do I build a golden dataset if I don't have labeled data?"
•  "Where is most of my cost actually going in a multi-agent system?"
•  "Do guardrails hurt latency and user experience?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Observability (what happened) and evaluation (was it good) are distinct and both required.
2.  Guardrails are layered — input and output, multiple techniques — not a single filter.
3.  Evaluation needs a reference: golden datasets and clear metrics beat vibes.
4.  Cost is an engineering metric you design against, not a surprise on the invoice.
5.  Trustworthiness is built in, through instrumentation, not bolted on at the end.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "LLM-as-judge is unreliable because it's circular." Clarify that a judge with a rubric, examples, and a different role than the generator is a validated, widely-used technique — imperfect but far better than nothing.
•  "Observability and evaluation are the same." Clarify: observability tells you what the agent did; evaluation tells you whether it was good.
•  "Guardrails are just content moderation." Clarify they also cover format validation, PII, injection defense, and business-rule enforcement.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive able to build powerful systems that are hard to trust or debug. Today is where the program's engineering conscience lands: trace everything, evaluate systematically, guard inputs and outputs, and measure cost. The mindset from Week 3 (measure then improve) now applies to whole agent systems. Keep the observability-vs-evaluation distinction sharp, and address the LLM-as-judge skepticism head-on — it's the objection that derails this class. Everything from here is about operating systems well: the two LLMOps inserts, the fine-tuning evaluation, and the capstone all assume these skills. Frame today as the transition from "can I build it?" to "can I run it responsibly and afford it?"

Week 8(a).title: LLMOps Part 1: Operating AI Systems in Production
Week 8(a).content:
SWE Module 8(a) — LLMOps Part 1: Operating AI Systems in Production

1. Course Journey This short insert exists to give learners the operational vocabulary that Weeks 8 through 9 assume: what "Ops" means, how MLOps evolved, and how LLMOps differs. It sits immediately after observability/evaluation because those are the raw materials of an ops practice. It moves learners toward the capstone by reframing everything they've built as a system to be operated, not just a program to be run.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W8 — Observability: LangSmith setup and tracing, the debugging workflow (wrong answer → open trace → find the fault), and monitoring, tagging and production sampling.
•  W8 — Evaluation: custom evaluators, LLM-as-judge for faithfulness and correctness, MRR, A/B experiments and hill-climbing in LangSmith, and DeepEval/G-Eval wired into CI/CD.
•  W8 — Guardrails and cost: layered guardrails (regex input guard, Moderation API, Presidio PII redaction, Guardrails AI, LLM-based injection detection) and GDPR/HIPAA patterns; token economics with tiktoken, the before/after methodology, semantic caching, audit logging and the cost–quality Pareto frontier.
•  W4–W7 — End-to-end agent systems: LangGraph orchestration, voice and HITL, MCP/ADK/A2A and hybrid retrieval — the kinds of systems an ops practice must run.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System (in progress): a production-grade support system hardened in four passes: observability (traces, runs, run trees, debugging, monitoring, sampling), evaluation (datasets, evaluators, MRR, DeepEval vs LangSmith, G-Eval), guardrails (Regex → Moderation → ML/NER → LLM, Guardrails AI, Presidio, GDPR/HIPAA) and cost (token economics, before/after methodology, four optimization patterns).
     Callback: hold it up as the system an ops practice would run — they already own its instruments.
•  W8 Assignment — Observability, evaluation, guardrails and cost: LangSmith and DeepEval tracing and custom metrics; multi-layer input/output guardrails; token tracking, semantic caching, structured logging, audit trails, budget monitoring and quality regression testing.
•  W7 Project — PubMedQA Hybrid Search: dense-only vs sparse-only vs hybrid (RRF) retrieval in Qdrant.
•  Earlier builds: Real Estate Negotiation and the MCP/ADK/A2A exercises (W6); AxiomCart and SnackStack (W5); Travel Planner and Content Writer (W4); SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: articulate the "Ops mindset" (reliability, repeatability, monitoring, iteration); explain what MLOps established and why; and describe how LLMOps extends and differs from classic MLOps (prompts as artifacts, non-determinism, eval-driven deployment). They leave able to talk about their systems in production/operational terms, grounded by a demo.

4. What this prepares learners for This vocabulary is the frame for W9 fine-tuning (which needs deployment/versioning thinking) and LLMOps Part 2 (W9a). It shapes how learners reason about the capstone as a deployable, maintainable system and underpins the productionization phases in the later deep dives.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Connect to Week 8: "the traces, evals, and cost metrics you just learned are the instruments an ops practice runs on."
•  Contrast with traditional software ops learners may know: "same discipline, new failure modes — non-determinism and prompt drift."
•  Foreshadow Week 9: "you can't fine-tune responsibly without versioning and deployment discipline — that's LLMOps."
•  Note that the capstone's grade partly reflects whether it's built like something operable, not just demo-able.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How is LLMOps different from the DevOps/MLOps I already know?"
•  "Why is non-determinism such a big deal operationally?"
•  "Is a prompt really an 'artifact' I need to version?"
•  "Do I need all this ops machinery for a small project?"
•  "Where does evaluation fit in a deployment pipeline?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Ops is a mindset — reliability, monitoring, iteration — before it's tooling.
2.  LLMOps inherits from MLOps but adds non-determinism and prompt/version management.
3.  Evaluation is part of the deployment loop, not a separate activity.
4.  Prompts, datasets, and eval suites are versioned artifacts.
5.  "It runs" and "it's operable" are different bars.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "LLMOps is just MLOps rebranded." Clarify the genuinely new problems: non-determinism, prompt/version drift, eval-gated releases.
•  "Ops is only for large teams." Clarify the mindset scales down; even a solo project benefits from monitoring and versioned prompts.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is a short framing module: give learners the operational language to describe what they've built. They arrive fluent in building and evaluating agents; today they learn to see those agents as systems that must be deployed, monitored, and iterated — the Ops mindset, MLOps lineage, and what LLMOps adds on top. The one idea to leave them with is that evaluation is part of the release loop, not a final polish. This sets up fine-tuning next week (which demands versioning and deployment discipline) and the capstone's expectation that systems be operable, not just demoable.

Week 9.title: Fine-Tuning & Domain Adaptation
Week 9.content:
SWE Module 9 — Fine-Tuning & Domain Adaptation

1. Course Journey Every previous fix changed the system around the model — better prompts, retrieval, orchestration, guardrails. This module exists for the cases those can't solve: when you need to change the model's behavior itself. It appears late deliberately, so learners first exhaust the cheaper levers (prompting, RAG, hybrid search) and can reason about when fine-tuning is actually the right tool. This is the "reach into the model" week, and it closes the technical arc before the capstone.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W2–W3, W7 — Knowledge levers: RAG (embeddings, chunking, Chroma, pipelines, Agentic RAG) and hybrid retrieval (dense + sparse vectors, SPLADE, HNSW, RRF in Qdrant) — the cheaper fixes to rule out before training.
•  W1 — Prompt engineering: the first of the three domain-adaptation approaches (prompting, RAG, fine-tuning) compared today.
•  W3, W8 — Evaluation: RAG metrics, LangSmith datasets and custom evaluators, LLM-as-judge, A/B experiments and DeepEval/G-Eval — today's "metrics over vibes" step reuses them directly.
•  W8 — Cost economics: token economics, before/after measurement and the cost–quality Pareto frontier.
•  W8(a) — LLMOps Part 1: the Ops mindset; MLOps vs LLMOps vs AgentOps; the AI system lifecycle; prompt versioning, model selection and routing, exact and semantic caching, guardrails, HITL patterns and LLM observability — demoed on a production-style travel agent with Langfuse.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: traced, evaluated, guarded and cost-optimized.
     Callback: their LangSmith evaluators and before/after methodology are exactly how today's base-vs-fine-tuned comparison gets settled.
•  W8 Assignment — Trust toolkit: observability, evaluation, guardrail and cost pipelines (LangSmith, DeepEval, Presidio, Guardrails AI, semantic caching, audit trails, regression tests).
•  W7 Project — PubMedQA Hybrid Search: dense vs sparse vs hybrid retrieval over biomedical abstracts.
     Callback: today's project is also medical — ask whether a weak medical answer is a knowledge problem (retrieval) or a behavior problem (fine-tuning) before anyone trains.
•  Earlier builds: Real Estate Negotiation and the MCP/ADK/A2A exercises (W6); AxiomCart and SnackStack (W5); Travel Planner and Content Writer (W4); SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: audit and prepare datasets and judge data quality before training; run QLoRA fine-tuning (e.g. on Colab); deploy and serve adapters efficiently (HF, adapter toggling with no extra VRAM); and evaluate fine-tuned vs base models with LangSmith ("metrics over vibes"); plus estimate deployment cost. They leave able to decide on, execute, and evaluate a fine-tune, evidenced by the fine-tuning project.

4. What this prepares learners for Fine-tuning completes the learner's decision toolkit for the capstone: prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune. The dataset-quality and QLoRA reasoning underpin LLMOps Part 2 (W9a) and the optimization/model-selection thinking in the deep dives. The base-vs-fine-tuned evaluation discipline is a direct application of Week 8's evaluation frameworks.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the whole module as a decision: "Weeks 2, 3, and 7 were about knowledge; today is about behavior. Ask which one your problem needs before you train."
•  Callback to Week 7: "before fine-tuning to fix bad answers, did hybrid retrieval already fix them cheaper?"
•  Tie "metrics over vibes" straight to Week 8: "same evaluation frameworks, now comparing two models."
•  Connect QLoRA/adapters to Week 8a's cost and deployment concerns.
•  Preview that model selection and GPU sizing get revisited in the optimization deep dives.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When do I fine-tune instead of using RAG or better prompts?"
•  "What is QLoRA and why does it make fine-tuning affordable?"
•  "How much data do I actually need, and how good does it have to be?"
•  "Will fine-tuning make the model forget things (catastrophic forgetting)?"
•  "How do I prove the fine-tuned model is actually better?"
•  "What does it cost to serve a fine-tuned model in production?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Fine-tuning changes behavior/style, not knowledge — RAG is still the tool for knowledge.
2.  Data quality dominates outcomes — audit before you train.
3.  QLoRA/adapters make fine-tuning cheap enough to be a real option, not just a research luxury.
4.  Base-vs-fine-tuned must be settled with metrics, not impressions.
5.  Fine-tuning is one tool in a decision hierarchy — usually the last one to reach for.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Fine-tuning is how you add knowledge to a model." Clarify that fine-tuning teaches behavior/format/style; for facts, use retrieval. This is the pivotal distinction of the module.
•  "More data always helps." Clarify that a small, clean, well-targeted dataset often beats a large noisy one.
•  "Fine-tuning is too expensive/advanced for real projects." Clarify that QLoRA and adapters have made it broadly accessible.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive having fixed problems by improving the system around the model. Today they learn to change the model itself — and, more importantly, when that's the right move. Protect the central distinction: fine-tuning shapes behavior and style; RAG supplies knowledge. Reinforce that data quality, not volume, decides success, and that QLoRA/adapters make this a practical, affordable option. Everything connects to earlier weeks: it's a decision built on top of prompting, RAG, and hybrid search, evaluated with Week 8's frameworks, deployed with Week 8a's discipline. This closes the technical curriculum — next comes the capstone, where all these levers get used together on one shipped system.

Week 9(a).title: LLMOps Part 2: Production Readiness
Week 9(a).content:
SWE Module 9(a) — LLMOps Part 2: Production Readiness

1. Course Journey Part 1 gave the ops mindset; this insert makes it concrete for agents specifically. It exists to consolidate AgentOps, evals, reliability, and cost into a production-readiness checklist right before the capstone. It's positioned here so learners walk into their capstone thinking like operators, not just builders.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W8 — The trust toolkit: tracing and the debugging workflow, evaluators and CI/CD evals, layered guardrails, token tracking, semantic caching and audit logging.
•  W8(a) — LLMOps Part 1: the Ops mindset, the seven production failure modes unique to AI, the AI system lifecycle, prompt versioning, model routing, caching, HITL patterns and Langfuse observability.
•  W9 — Fine-tuning and domain adaptation: the prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune decision framework; full fine-tuning vs PEFT (LoRA, QLoRA, prefix tuning, adapter layers, IA3); QLoRA internals (4-bit NF4, double quantization); dataset sourcing and the chat format; SFTTrainer and hyperparameters; adapter deployment on Hugging Face (adapter toggle, merge decision, four deployment strategies, scale-to-zero); LangSmith evaluation of base vs fine-tuned.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W9 Project — Healthcare QLoRA Fine-Tuning Pipeline (in progress): two controlled QLoRA experiments fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a free Colab T4, each up to three epochs, each ending in a documented improvement or a reproducible regression — across strategy and dataset prep, QLoRA training, Hugging Face deploy and inference, and LangSmith evaluation.
     Callback: in class, v1 (ChatDoctor) regressed on all three metrics while v2 (WikiDoc) was mixed — a ready-made case for regression testing and eval-gated releases.
•  W9 Assignment — Fine-tuning analysis: dataset quality audits, prompt engineering vs fine-tuning comparisons, LoRA/hyperparameter and dataset-size trade-offs, generation-parameter tests, base vs fine-tuned comparisons, deployment-cost estimates and custom evaluation metrics.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: the trust toolkit in one build.
     Callback: today's AgentOps checklist is what would take it from hardened demo to production service.
•  W4 Project — Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System: their own multi-agent travel planner.
     Callback: today's demo hardens a prototype travel agent — the same domain as this project and the 8(a) demo — so each production fix maps onto a design they have already built.
•  Earlier builds: PubMedQA hybrid search (W7); Real Estate Negotiation (W6); AxiomCart and SnackStack (W5); Content Writer (W4); SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: apply AgentOps practices to multi-step agent systems; treat evals & quality as a continuous, gating process; design for reliability (retries, fallbacks, failure isolation) and manage cost at scale. They leave with a mental production-readiness checklist, grounded by a demo.

4. What this prepares learners for Directly de-risks the capstone and defines what "production-ready" means for it. The reliability and cost themes are load-bearing in every advanced deep dive (W12–W15), where productionization is an explicit phase.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Tie together the whole trust arc: "Week 8 gave you the instruments, 8a the mindset, today the checklist."
•  Connect reliability patterns to Week 6's server-failure recovery and self-correction — "same instincts, system-wide now."
•  Frame cost-at-scale as the grown-up version of Week 4's "more agents cost more."
•  Tell them explicitly: "your capstone will be judged partly on these production concerns."

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "What does 'production-ready' actually mean for an agent?"
•  "How do I make a non-deterministic system reliable?"
•  "How often should evals run — every deploy, continuously?"
•  "What's the biggest cost trap in agent systems at scale?"
•  "How is AgentOps different from the LLMOps we just covered?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Reliability for agents means designing for failure — retries, fallbacks, isolation.
2.  Evals are continuous and gating, not one-time.
3.  Cost management is an architectural concern at scale.
4.  AgentOps applies ops discipline to multi-step, non-deterministic systems.
5.  Production readiness is a checklist you can articulate and defend.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "If it passes evals once, it's production-ready." Clarify that quality drifts; evals must run continuously.
•  "Reliability is about better prompts." Clarify it's about system design — fallbacks, retries, graceful degradation.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This short capstone-launch module consolidates the trust arc into production readiness for agents: AgentOps, continuous evals, reliability, and cost at scale. Learners arrive with the instruments (Week 8), the mindset (8a), and fine-tuning experience (Week 9); today they get the checklist that ties it together. The one idea to leave them with is that reliability in a non-deterministic system is a design problem — retries, fallbacks, isolation — not a prompting problem. Send them into the capstone thinking like operators. Everything they build over the next two weeks should be defensible against these production concerns.

Weeks 10–11.title: Capstone Project Sessions
Weeks 10–11.content:
SWE Modules 10–11 — Capstone Project Sessions

1. Course Journey The capstone exists to force integration: nine weeks of separately-taught capabilities must now fuse into one coherent, operable system. It sits here because learners finally hold the full toolkit — agents, RAG, orchestration, protocols, evaluation, ops, fine-tuning — and the only way to prove mastery is to ship. It's the bridge between "learned the pieces" and "can build a system," and the reference point the later interview deep dives assume.

2. What learners already know Effectively the entire curriculum — plus a portfolio of builds that each capstone option extends.
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1–W9(a) — The full toolkit: agents and tools (W1); RAG and evaluation (W2–W3); LangGraph multi-agent systems (W4); voice, sub-graphs and HITL (W5); MCP, ADK and A2A (W6); hybrid search (W7); observability, evaluation, guardrails and cost (W8); LLMOps Parts 1–2 (W8a, W9a); fine-tuning (W9).
•  Claude Code floater session (if already held for this cohort): spec-driven development vs "vibe coding," context engineering, the BMAD method and its artifact chain (product brief → PRD → architecture → stories), CLAUDE.md as project memory, and MCP inside Claude Code — directly useful for scoping and building a capstone.
Prior builds each capstone option extends
•  AI Finance Assistant (Finnie): six LangGraph agents grounded in RAG, delivering investment guidance, market insights, portfolio analysis, goal planning and tax education.
     Builds on: the Financial Bot (W3, optional), SupportDesk-RAG (W2–W3) and the multi-agent orchestration of the Travel Planner (W4).
•  AI Content Marketing Assistant (ContentAlchemy): multi-agent blogs, LinkedIn posts, visuals and research-driven content with SEO optimization and brand-voice consistency.
     Builds on: the Multi-Agent Content Writer (W4) — SEO Blog and X/Twitter writers with research tools and checkpointer memory.
•  Call Center Intelligence System: a seven-stage LangGraph pipeline with faster-whisper speech-to-text, speaker diarization, PII redaction, prompt-injection defense and a weighted QA scorecard.
     Builds on: AxiomCart's voice I/O and the audio reading on diarization (W5), plus the FinTech guardrails (Presidio, injection detection) and evaluators (W8).
•  Multi-Agent Customer Support Assistant: a supervisor over specialist agents answering from a live relational database, with identity verification and per-customer preference memory.
     Builds on: the W4 supervisor/router pattern and Memory Store, SnackStack and AxiomCart (W5), and the FinTech support system (W8).
•  SmartDesk AI (IT & HR operations agent): RAG plus multi-agent orchestration with Jira/Asana/Notion ticketing, confidence-based escalation and human-confirmed ticket creation.
     Builds on: the Autonomous IT Support Agent (W1), SupportDesk-RAG (W2–W3), HITL (W5) and MCP integrations (W6).
•  BYOP: any idea — ask each learner to name the two prior projects it extends; if they can't, the scope is probably unanchored.

3. What learners will learn today Across the sessions learners will: scope a real system (AI Finance Assistant, Content Marketing Assistant, Call Center Intelligence, Multi-Agent Customer Support, SmartDesk IT/HR agent, or BYOP); make explicit architecture decisions (single vs multi-agent, RAG vs fine-tune, which protocols); instrument it for observability and evaluation; add guardrails; and defend cost and reliability tradeoffs. They leave with a portfolio-grade, end-to-end agentic system.

4. What this prepares learners for The capstone is the concrete artifact the interview-prep deep dives (W12–W15) abstract from. Every design decision made here — coordination, verification, retrieval, productionization — is exactly what those sessions rehearse at whiteboard/interview depth. It's also the primary portfolio piece for job search.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Push learners to justify each choice against earlier weeks: "Why multi-agent here? Why RAG over fine-tuning? Where are your guardrails?"
•  When they hit orchestration pain, point back to Week 4 state and Week 5 sub-graphs.
•  When answers are wrong, send them to Week 3/7/8 (retrieval and evaluation), not to more prompting.
•  Frame the capstone as interview material: "you'll re-tell these decisions in Weeks 12–15 as system-design answers."
•  Reinforce production readiness (9a) as a grading lens, not an afterthought.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Is BYOP risky compared to a guided track?"
•  "How much do I need to build versus polish?"
•  "Do I have to use every technique from the course?"
•  "How production-ready does it realistically need to be?"
•  "How do I show my architecture decisions, not just the working demo?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Architecture is a series of justified decisions, not a pile of features.
2.  Use the least powerful tool that solves the problem (prompt < RAG < multi-agent < fine-tune).
3.  Observability and evaluation are part of the deliverable, not extras.
4.  Cost and reliability tradeoffs must be explicit and defensible.
5.  The story of why you built it this way matters as much as the demo.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "More techniques = better capstone." Clarify that unjustified complexity is a negative signal; restraint and rationale win.
•  "The demo is the deliverable." Clarify that decisions, evaluation, and operability are what distinguish a strong capstone.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is integration under pressure. Learners hold the whole toolkit and must now fuse it into one operable system and — just as importantly — justify every choice. Your highest-value coaching is forcing rationale: why this architecture, why RAG over fine-tuning, where the guardrails and evals are, what it costs. Redirect "make it smarter" instincts back to retrieval and evaluation rather than more prompting or more agents. Remind them the capstone isn't just a portfolio demo — it's the raw material they'll narrate as senior-level system-design answers in the next four weeks. Reward restraint and defensible decisions over feature count.
