Week 12.title: Agentic Research Systems: Planning, Tools & Guardrails
Week 12.content:
SWE Module 12 (W12) — Agentic Research Systems: Planning, Tools & Guardrails

1. Course Journey This deep dive exists to rehearse designing a research agent — one that plans multi-step investigations, uses tools, remembers, and stays guarded — at interview depth. It comes after the capstone because it presumes learners can already build such systems; now they practice defending the design. It moves them toward the job-search finish line, where system-design fluency, not just working code, is what's assessed.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1 — Planning and the agent loop: ReAct, planning and reasoning, agentic design patterns — today's refresh extends these to Plan-and-Execute, hybrids, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts and CodeAct.
•  W1, W6 — Tools: function calling and MCP (primitives, transports, multiple servers, automatic tool discovery, failure recovery and LLM self-correction).
•  W2–W3, W7 — Retrieval: embeddings, chunking, indexing, RAG evaluation, and hybrid dense + sparse search with RRF — the research agent's retrieval module.
•  W1, W4 — Memory: short- vs long-term memory, LangGraph checkpointers and the Memory Store.
•  W8, W8(a), W9(a) — Trust and production: tracing, evaluators, LLM-as-judge, layered guardrails including prompt-injection detection, and cost tracking; retries, circuit breakers, fallback chains and graceful degradation.
Projects and assignments already built
•  Capstone (W10–11): their own end-to-end system — the richest source of "I already made this decision" answers.
     Callback: ask each learner to bring one planning, one memory and one guardrail decision from it.
•  W4 Project — Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System: answered travel questions with deep research and ran multiple queries in parallel — the closest earlier build to a research agent.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: a traced, evaluated, guarded multi-agent system — their reference for Phase 4 (observability + feedback) and Phase 5 (testing).
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: retrieval and generation metrics plus Agentic RAG — the grounding and citation story behind research-agent guardrails.
•  Also relevant: PubMedQA hybrid search over research abstracts (W7); Real Estate Negotiation over MCP data with A2A (W6).

3. What learners will learn today Working through six phases — fundamentals refresh, system design, memory design, observability + feedback, testing strategy, productionization — learners will be able to: architect a research agent from a blank prompt; justify memory and tool choices; design guardrails and feedback loops; and articulate a productionization path. They leave able to whiteboard a research-agent design end to end.

4. What this prepares learners for This is terminal interview preparation, but it also reinforces patterns reused in Text-to-SQL (W13) and Multi-Agent Coordination (W14) — planning, tool design, and guardrails are shared vocabulary across all three.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Anchor every phase to a capstone decision: "you already made this choice — now say why out loud."
•  Tie memory design to Week 2's short/long-term memory and vector stores.
•  Tie guardrails and feedback to Week 8's observability and evaluation.
•  Frame productionization against LLMOps (W8a/9a).
•  Note that the phase structure itself is a reusable interview framework.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How deep should I go on each phase in a 45-minute interview?"
•  "How do I choose memory architecture on the spot?"
•  "What guardrails do interviewers expect me to mention?"
•  "How is a research agent different from a RAG system?"
•  "What's a strong answer for 'how would you productionize this'?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  System design is a structured conversation — the phases are a framework, not a script.
2.  Every choice needs a stated tradeoff.
3.  Memory and guardrails are where weak candidates go silent — over-prepare them.
4.  Feedback loops distinguish a toy from a system.
5.  Productionization thinking signals seniority.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "System design is about naming tools." Clarify it's about justified tradeoffs and failure handling.
•  "A research agent is just RAG." Clarify it adds planning, multi-step tool use, and iterative refinement.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive able to build research agents; this session makes them able to defend the design under interview pressure. Walk the six phases as a reusable framework and force a stated tradeoff at every step, especially on memory and guardrails, where candidates typically stall. Anchor everything to concrete capstone decisions so it's recall, not invention. The goal isn't new capability — it's fluency and structure. This is the first of four interview rehearsals; the planning/tools/guardrails vocabulary here recurs across the next three.

Week 13.title: Agentic Text-to-SQL: Reliable Data Reasoning Systems
Week 13.content:
SWE Module 13 (W13) — Agentic Text-to-SQL: Reliable Data Reasoning Systems

1. Course Journey This deep dive tackles one of the hardest, most-asked interview problems: an agent that turns natural language into reliable SQL over real schemas. It exists because Text-to-SQL concentrates almost every course theme — retrieval (schema), sub-agents, tool design, guardrails, self-correction, evaluation — into one high-stakes problem where being wrong is worse than being silent. It comes late because it assumes command of all those pieces.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W7 — Hybrid retrieval: sparse (inverted index, SPLADE) and dense vectors fused with RRF — today's schema retrieval combines BM25 and dense embeddings with other signals in a five-signal funnel.
•  W4 — Sub-agents and LangGraph state machines: routing, sub-agents and when not to use them — the basis for today's sub-agent topology and self-correction state machine.
•  W6 — MCP and self-correction: MCP servers and tool contracts, server-failure recovery and LLM self-correction — today's execute_sql tool sits behind read-only and read-write MCP servers.
•  W8 — Guardrails, evaluation and cost: layered guardrails and injection defense, LLM-as-judge, CI/CD evals and cost tracking.
•  W12 — Deep dive: Agentic Research Systems: the phased interview framework; ReAct vs Plan-and-Execute; tool failure modes; layered prompt-injection defense; memory trade-offs; the limits of LLM-as-judge; and productionization (invocation patterns, circuit breakers, caching).
Projects and assignments already built
•  W12 — Market Research Report Generator (whiteboard design): designed last week, from requirements through productionization.
     Callback: today repeats that cadence — requirements, architecture, failure modes, guardrails, evaluation, production — under a much stricter reliability bar.
•  W7 Project — PubMedQA Hybrid Search: hands-on proof that lexical plus semantic retrieval beats either alone.
     Callback: table and column names behave like the exact identifiers sparse vectors caught in that project.
•  Capstone — Multi-Agent Customer Support Assistant (if chosen): supervisor-routed agents answering over a live relational database with anti-hallucination grounding — learners who built it have already met today's problem at small scale.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: layered guardrails and custom evaluators — the base for today's AST validator, policy-as-code checks and CI eval gate.
•  W6 Assignment — MCP exercises: multi-server tool discovery, server-failure recovery and LLM self-correction — the base for today's retry decision tree.

3. What learners will learn today Across nine phases (framing, pipeline & cost math, schema retrieval, semantic layer & sub-agent topology, tool design, guardrails, self-correction & retry, evaluation & observability, productionization at scale), learners will be able to: design a Text-to-SQL system that retrieves the right schema, decomposes work across sub-agents, guards against unsafe/incorrect queries, self-corrects on failure, and is evaluated and cost-modeled. They leave able to defend a production-grade data-reasoning system.

4. What this prepares learners for Terminal interview prep. It also crystallizes the self-correction/retry pattern that the Self-Improving Agents deep dive (W15) generalizes, and the schema retrieval pattern that reuses hybrid search from W7.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Tie schema retrieval directly to Week 7 hybrid search: "exact table/column names are a lexical-match problem."
•  Connect sub-agent topology to Week 4 orchestration.
•  Tie guardrails to Week 8 and to the cost of a wrong query executing against production data.
•  Connect self-correction to Week 6's LLM self-correction patterns.
•  Frame the cost math phase against LLMOps cost thinking.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Why is Text-to-SQL so much harder than normal RAG?"
•  "How does the agent retrieve the right schema without loading the whole database?"
•  "What guardrails stop a destructive or wrong query?"
•  "How does self-correction work when the SQL fails?"
•  "How do I evaluate correctness when there are many valid queries?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Reliability is the whole game — a confidently wrong query is the worst outcome.
2.  Schema retrieval is a retrieval problem (and hybrid search shines here).
3.  Sub-agent decomposition tames complexity.
4.  Self-correction/retry turns failures into recoveries.
5.  Correctness evaluation is subtle — multiple valid answers exist.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Text-to-SQL is just prompting the model with the schema." Clarify why schema retrieval, guardrails, and self-correction are essential at real scale.
•  "If the SQL runs, it's correct." Clarify that executable and correct are different — evaluation must check semantics.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Text-to-SQL is the course's capstone problem in miniature — retrieval, sub-agents, guardrails, self-correction, evaluation, and cost, all under a strict reliability bar. Learners arrive with every piece; today they assemble and defend them for a problem where being wrong beats being silent only in the sense that both are failures. Anchor schema retrieval to Week 7 hybrid search and self-correction to Week 6. The nine phases are dense — prioritize framing, schema retrieval, guardrails, and self-correction if time is short. Emphasize that reliability, not cleverness, is what interviewers probe. Next up: coordinating many agents.

Week 14.title: Multi-Agent Systems: Coordination & Shared Intelligence
Week 14.content:
SWE Module 14 (W14) — Multi-Agent Systems: Coordination & Shared Intelligence

1. Course Journey Week 4 taught learners to build multi-agent systems; this deep dive teaches them to reason rigorously about coordination — roles, contracts, topology, shared state, and the failure modes that emerge when agents depend on each other. It exists because "add more agents" is where naive designs break, and interviewers probe exactly that. It comes late because it presumes fluency with orchestration, MCP/A2A, and reliability.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W4 — LangGraph multi-agent systems: State, persistence, the Memory Store, supervisor/router patterns, sub-agents and when not to use them.
•  W5 — Sub-graphs and HITL: composing sub-graphs and pausing on interrupts for human approval — the seed of today's "HITL on every destructive action."
•  W6 — A2A and Google ADK: Agent Cards, context threading, parts and artifacts; Sequential, Parallel and Loop agents, Agent-as-Tool and callbacks; negotiation orchestration under information asymmetry.
•  W8, W9(a) — Reliability, cost and evaluation: retries, timeouts and circuit breakers, fallback chains, graceful degradation, rate limiting and budget caps; per-agent tracing and routing-accuracy evaluators.
•  W12–W13 — Deep dives 1–2: the eight-stage interview framework (restate, requirements, topology, tools, failure modes, eval, scaling, trade-offs); Plan-and-Execute vs ReAct; sub-agent topology and model selection; self-consistency; six-layer defense in depth.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W4 builds — Travel Planner and Multi-Agent Content Writer: their first supervisor/router designs, with parallel queries and checkpointer memory.
     Callback: ask what each specialist was allowed to read and write — today turns that implicit agreement into typed role contracts and a permission matrix.
•  W5 Project — AxiomCart: an orchestrator routing to a Product Agent sub-graph and a Support Agent, joined by a synthesizer, with HITL — a concrete supervisor, join and human gate.
•  W6 Project — Real Estate Negotiation Workshop: Buyer and Seller agents under an ADK negotiation orchestrator over A2A; the W6 exercises added negotiation-stall detection, hierarchical delegation and shared memory.
     Callback: stall detection is a termination guarantee — the fourth of today's coordination primitives.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: per-agent tracing plus routing_accuracy and keyword_correctness evaluators — the starting point for today's multi-agent evaluation view.
•  Capstone: several tracks are multi-agent (Finnie's six agents, the Customer Support supervisor, ContentAlchemy, SmartDesk).
     Callback: ask learners to redraw theirs using today's four coordination primitives.

3. What learners will learn today Across its phases (clarify, architecture, coordination via agent roles & contracts, coordination topology, shared intelligence, reliability/execution, coordination failure modes, scale, production concerns, tradeoffs), learners will be able to: define agent roles and contracts; choose a coordination topology; design shared intelligence/state; and anticipate and mitigate coordination failure modes at scale. They leave able to defend a multi-agent architecture — including where it shouldn't be multi-agent.

4. What this prepares learners for Terminal interview prep. Consolidates the multi-agent thread that began at W4 and ran through A2A (W6), and pairs with Self-Improving Agents (W15) as the two "advanced systems" interviews.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback to Week 4: "you built these; now define the contracts between them."
•  Tie A2A negotiation (W6) to formal coordination topology here.
•  Connect failure modes to Week 8/9a reliability.
•  Repeatedly ask "would a single agent be simpler?" — the strongest answers know when not to go multi-agent.
•  Frame shared intelligence as the grown-up version of LangGraph state.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When is multi-agent genuinely better than one strong agent?"
•  "What's an 'agent contract' and why does it matter?"
•  "How do coordination failures actually happen?"
•  "How do agents share state reliably at scale?"
•  "How do I discuss tradeoffs without sounding hand-wavy?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Coordination needs explicit roles and contracts, not vibes.
2.  Topology is a design choice with real consequences.
3.  Multi-agent systems fail in new ways — plan for coordination failure.
4.  Knowing when not to use multi-agent is a seniority signal.
5.  Shared intelligence is disciplined shared state.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Multi-agent is always more capable." Clarify the coordination tax and failure surface; sometimes one agent wins.
•  "Agents coordinate automatically." Clarify that contracts, topology, and shared state are deliberately engineered.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is the rigorous sequel to Week 4. Learners can already wire agents together; today they reason about roles, contracts, topology, shared intelligence, and — the part interviews love — coordination failure modes. The single most valuable habit to instill is asking "would one agent be simpler?" before defending a multi-agent design; candidates who default to more agents look junior. Anchor to Week 4 state and Week 6 A2A. Emphasize that multi-agent systems fail in ways single agents don't, and that anticipating those failures is what separates a strong answer from a feature list. One deep dive remains: agents that evaluate and improve themselves.

Week 15.title: Self-Improving Agents: Evaluation & Verification Loops
Week 15.content:
SWE Module 15 (W15) — Self-Improving Agents: Evaluation & Verification Loops

1. Course Journey The final deep dive closes the loop the whole course has been building toward: agents that verify their own work and improve. Using a code-review system as the anchor, it generalizes evaluation (W3, W8) into verification loops, LLM-as-judge, and online/offline feedback. It exists because self-verification is the frontier of reliable agentic systems and a favorite hard interview topic. It's last because it requires mastery of evaluation, reliability, and multi-agent design.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W3, W8 — Evaluation: Precision/Recall/F1, groundedness, LLM-as-judge (faithfulness, correctness), custom evaluators, MRR, A/B experiments and hill-climbing, DeepEval/G-Eval in CI/CD.
•  W9 — Before/after evaluation: base vs fine-tuned comparisons with LangSmith evaluators for helpfulness, accuracy and safety — including a real regression.
•  W9(a) — Continuous evals: task- vs system-level evaluation, automated vs human review, regression testing in CI/CD, golden and synthetic datasets, and the trust scorecard.
•  W13 — Verification in miniature: AST validation, dry-run/EXPLAIN, self-consistency (choosing K), monthly LLM-judge calibration and CI eval gates.
•  W14 — Coordination: role contracts, supervisor topology, typed shared state and the Critic as an online judge — today's "reviewers as a multi-agent system" builds directly on it.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W14 — Personal Task Execution System (PTES) design: five agents (Planner, Researcher, Decision, Executor, Critic) under a supervisor, with a permission matrix and HITL on destructive actions.
     Callback: PTES's Critic is today's verification loop in embryo.
•  W9 Project — Healthcare QLoRA Fine-Tuning Pipeline: controlled experiments that had to end in a documented improvement or a reproducible regression; in class, v1 (ChatDoctor) regressed on all three metrics.
     Callback: a real case of why verification beats impressions.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: custom evaluators (routing_accuracy, keyword_correctness), LLM-as-judge for faithfulness and correctness, and DeepEval in CI — the offline-evaluation half of today's design.
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: where "measure, then improve" started; today's golden dataset and per-category precision/recall are the same ideas at production scale.
•  Capstone: each learner's own evaluation and observability plan.
     Callback: ask what theirs caught — and what it missed.

3. What learners will learn today Across its phases (clarify, architecture, context & grounding, the reviewers, signal fusion, why verification is hard, offline evaluation, the verification loop, verifying correctness, LLM-as-judge, online evaluation & feedback, reliability & scale, tradeoffs), learners will be able to: design multiple reviewer agents, fuse their signals, build offline and online verification loops, use LLM-as-judge responsibly, and reason about why verification is genuinely hard. They leave able to defend a self-improving agent architecture.

4. What this prepares learners for Terminal interview prep and the conceptual summit of the program — it ties evaluation, multi-agent design, and reliability into one system. Nothing depends on it downstream; it's the capstone of the interview sequence.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame it as the natural end of the evaluation thread from Week 3 and Week 8.
•  Tie multiple reviewers + signal fusion to Week 14 coordination.
•  Revisit the LLM-as-judge skepticism from Week 8 and resolve it with rubric/grounding techniques.
•  Connect online feedback to LLMOps continuous-eval thinking.
•  Emphasize honesty about verification's limits — a mature, senior stance.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How can an agent reliably judge its own output?"
•  "Isn't LLM-as-judge circular — again?"
•  "What's the difference between offline and online evaluation here?"
•  "Why is verification harder than generation?"
•  "How do I fuse disagreeing reviewer signals?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Verification is harder than generation — respect that difficulty.
2.  Multiple reviewers plus signal fusion beat a single judge.
3.  Grounding and rubrics make LLM-as-judge defensible.
4.  Offline and online evaluation play different roles.
5.  Self-improvement is a loop: verify, learn, iterate.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "An agent can just check its own work." Clarify why naive self-checking fails and why grounded, multi-signal verification is needed.
•  "LLM-as-judge is unreliable, full stop." Clarify that with rubrics, grounding, and multiple judges it's a legitimate, widely-used technique.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is the program's conceptual summit: agents that verify and improve themselves. Learners arrive fluent in evaluation, multi-agent design, and reliability; today those threads converge into verification loops, multiple reviewers with signal fusion, LLM-as-judge done responsibly, and honest treatment of why verification is hard. Resolve the recurring LLM-as-judge skepticism decisively here. The senior stance to leave them with is intellectual honesty about verification's limits paired with concrete techniques to push past them. This completes the interview sequence — from here, learners are rehearsing, not learning. Send them out able to defend the hardest system in the course.

Week 0 (self-paced).title: Foundational Material & Pre-Program Foundations (self-paced orientation)
Week 0 (self-paced).content:
EM Module 0 — Foundational Material & Pre-Program Foundations (self-paced orientation)

Prerequisite scaffolding, not a live class.

What it covers: "Python for Non-Programmers" plus an optional AI exercise. The goal is literacy, not fluency — enough to read a workflow and reason about logic, not to ship production code.

Why it matters to you as an instructor: EMs often arrive rusty or non-coding. Set expectations early: they don't need to write much Python, but they must be able to follow logic, data flow, and conditionals, because every n8n workflow encodes exactly those. When workflows get complex in Weeks 3–5, learners who skipped this struggle to reason about branching and state. Frame Python literacy as the language for thinking about systems they'll build visually.

Week 1.title: Agentic Fundamentals (Reflex → Reasoning)
Week 1.content:
EM Module 1 (W1) — Agentic Fundamentals (Reflex → Reasoning)

1. Course Journey This is the atom of the program for EMs: the leap from a fixed rule to a reasoning agent, built visually in n8n. It exists so managers can see what an agent is — a loop that evaluates, decides, and acts — rather than treat it as a buzzword. It's first because every later module (RAG, orchestration, ops) is an extension of this loop, and because leading agentic teams starts with understanding the primitive.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  Module 0 — Python for Non-Programmers (self-paced): basics, NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib — enough literacy to follow logic, data flow and conditionals, the same constructs every n8n workflow encodes. Literacy, not fluency.
•  Pre-class primers for today: Prompting, Introduction to Agents, and LLM client libraries. Assume these were skimmed, not mastered.
•  Product-level AI familiarity: most EMs use AI tools and many know automation tools such as Zapier from their teams, but few have built an agent hands-on.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W0 Optional AI Exercise — BankCo premium-card retention agent: an internal agent for Relationship Managers: it reads connected spreadsheets, finds customers 30–90 days from annual-fee renewal who show disengagement signals, analyzes spend and experience signals, selects compliant retention offers from an Offer Policy, builds a prioritized customer list, drafts personalized outreach, logs recommendations and notifies the RM by email. Its solution walkthrough is part of this week's topic list.
     Callback: ask which steps followed fixed rules and which needed judgment — the judgment steps are what today's reasoning agent adds. The exercise was optional, so expect a mixed room: for many EMs, today's E-commerce Operations Agent is their first agent build.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain generative AI and LLMs and where they fail; write deliberate prompts; distinguish reflex/rule-based behavior from reasoning agents; and build a working agent in n8n that evaluates severity, maintains state to avoid duplicates, and emits structured decisions. Evidenced by the E-commerce Operations Agent that monitors checkout failures and publishes ALERT/LOG decisions via webhook.

4. What this prepares learners for The agent loop underpins RAG (W2), orchestration (W3), conversational agents (W4), and everything after. State management introduced here (avoiding duplicate processing) recurs in every workflow. The "map a business requirement to agent steps" instinct is the core managerial skill the whole track builds.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the reflex→reasoning jump as the difference between automation they already know and the agents they'll lead.
•  When you show state, note it recurs everywhere — "every workflow you build will manage state like this."
•  Foreshadow RAG: "this agent only knows its inputs; next week we give it a knowledge base."
•  Tie hallucination to why evaluation (W6) and guardrails exist.
•  Connect n8n nodes to the conceptual agent loop so the tool doesn't obscure the idea.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "As a manager, how much of this do I need to build myself?"
•  "How is an agent different from the automation/Zapier we already use?"
•  "When is an agent overkill versus a simple rule?"
•  "Can I trust an agent to make decisions autonomously?"
•  "Why n8n instead of writing code?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  An agent is a reasoning loop, not a fancy if-statement.
2.  State management is fundamental, not advanced.
3.  Business requirement → agent steps is the core skill.
4.  LLM limitations (hallucination) motivate everything downstream.
5.  Visual tools reveal the architecture; the concepts are what transfer.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Agents are just advanced automation." Clarify that reasoning and autonomous decision-making are a real category shift from rule-based flows.
•  "No-code means no architecture." Clarify that n8n workflows still embody real design decisions.

9. One-minute recap for instructors EMs arrive with product-level AI awareness but often little hands-on exposure. Today they build their first reasoning agent visually and, more importantly, learn to see the agent loop beneath the buzzwords. Keep them focused on the concept — evaluate, decide, act, remember — rather than n8n mechanics, and make sure they leave able to map a business need to agent steps. That translation skill is what makes them effective leaders of agentic projects. Plant the hallucination pain now; it's the seed for RAG next week and evaluation later. Everything ahead extends this single loop.

Week 2.title: RAG Knowledge Agents
Week 2.content:
EM Module 2 (W2) — RAG Knowledge Agents

1. Course Journey Last week's agent knew only its inputs. This module gives it grounded knowledge via retrieval, so it can answer from a real corpus rather than guess. It exists because most business agents EMs will oversee are fundamentally RAG systems, and managers must understand retrieval's moving parts to evaluate them. It's positioned right after the agent loop because grounding is the first and most important capability upgrade.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1 — Gen AI and LLM fundamentals: the evolution of AI, the SDLC becoming AI-driven, what Gen AI and LLMs are, prompt engineering, and the limitations of LLMs — hallucination above all.
•  W1 — Agents: agents and tools, agentic workflows vs autonomous agents, how EMs can leverage agents, and two design patterns: reflection and routing.
•  W1 — Post-class reading: LLM limitations → RAG motivation, LLM hallucinations, a bird's-eye view of Transformers, tools + memory + planning + ReAct, LangChain and OpenAI function calling — the RAG-motivation piece sets up today directly.
•  The gap they feel: their agent can only judge the data it is handed — it has no access to past incidents, policies or documents.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W1 Project and Assignment — E-commerce Operations Agent (n8n): reads new checkout events from Google Sheets, evaluates severity against baseline metrics, records the last processed timestamp so no alert is duplicated, outputs exactly one ALERT or LOG command per run, and broadcasts the decision to downstream systems via webhook. It publishes intent; it does not execute fixes.
     Callback: ask what it would need to answer "has this failure happened before, and what fixed it?" — that's today's knowledge base.
•  W0 Optional AI Exercise — BankCo retention agent: spreadsheet-driven decision support constrained by an Offer Policy.
     Callback: ask how it would cope if that policy were a 40-page PDF instead of a sheet — that is a retrieval problem.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain RAG and why it beats keyword search; reason about chunking and metadata design; understand embeddings and vector databases conceptually; ensure grounded responses via context injection; and build a RAG agent in n8n. Evidenced by the AI Finance Reporting Agent that retrieves from a vector DB, blends internal and external data, and emails a leadership report.

4. What this prepares learners for RAG is the knowledge substrate for orchestration (W3), a component to evaluate (W6), and a key node in the AI Product Architecture decisions echoed across the track. The RAG-vs-fine-tune question surfaces properly in W7.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback to Week 1: "the agent hallucinated because it had no source — RAG is the fix."
•  Keep embeddings-vs-vector-DB crisp; it's the classic confusion.
•  Note chunking/metadata quality caps answer quality — which they'll measure in Week 6.
•  Frame grounding as the manager's main lever for trustworthy outputs.
•  Preview that Week 7 asks when better retrieval beats fine-tuning.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "What's the difference between an embedding and a vector database?"
•  "How do I judge if a team's RAG system is any good?"
•  "Does RAG replace fine-tuning?"
•  "Why not just paste everything into the prompt?"
•  "How much does metadata design actually matter?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  RAG grounds answers in sources — the main defense against hallucination.
2.  Embeddings encode meaning; vector databases store and search them (not the same thing).
3.  Chunking and metadata quietly govern quality.
4.  Grounding is a leadership lever for trust.
5.  Retrieval quality is measurable — a theme for Week 6.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Embeddings and vector databases are the same." Clarify the distinction explicitly.
•  "RAG and fine-tuning compete." Clarify: knowledge vs behavior — different problems.

9. One-minute recap for instructors EMs come in having felt hallucination in their first agent. Today they learn the industry's standard remedy — retrieval-augmented generation — and how to reason about its parts well enough to evaluate a team's system. Keep the embeddings-vs-vector-database distinction sharp; it's the misconception that lingers. Emphasize that grounding is their primary lever for trustworthy outputs and that chunking and metadata silently determine quality. They leave able to build and assess a RAG agent. Next week single agents become coordinated teams of agents — with a critic to keep them honest.

Week 3.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
Week 3.content:
EM Module 3 (W3) — Multi-Agent Orchestration

1. Course Journey This module scales from one agent to a coordinated team: a Coordinator that routes, specialists that execute, and a Validator/Critic that checks. It exists because real business processes decompose across roles, and because the critic pattern is how managers get reliability from non-deterministic agents. It follows RAG because specialists often need grounded knowledge to do their jobs.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W2 — RAG foundations: types of agents, knowledge agents and their components, what RAG is, its benefits, when to use it, and the components of a RAG pipeline.
•  W2 — Chunking, metadata and embeddings: recursive and structure-aware chunking; overlap and one concept per chunk; chunk size and top-k as the two signal-vs-noise knobs; metadata design; query vs document embeddings, embedding limitations and cost/latency trade-offs — each with an EM Lens.
•  W2 — Vector databases and grounding: the vector-DB mental model and landscape, Pinecone, top-k and metadata filtering; grounding, Cohere Rerank, context injection, and safe handling of gaps, weak evidence and conflicts.
•  W1 — The agent loop: reasoning agents, state and structured decisions, and the reflection and routing patterns — routing returns today as the Coordinator's job.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W2 Project — RAG Intelligence Agent (n8n): ingests enterprise documents, generates embeddings and runs semantic retrieval to answer leadership questions with grounded, citation-backed insights — explaining business anomalies and producing metrics reports from verified internal sources only.
     Callback: ask what happens when one agent must retrieve, analyze, explain and report in a single flow — today splits those jobs across specialists.
•  W2 Assignment — AI Finance Reporting Agent: combines internal product performance data from a vector database with external market intelligence, analyzes industry trends, synthesizes insights and emails a leadership-ready monthly report.
     Callback: it already does several jobs — retrieve, analyze, write, deliver. Ask which they would hand to a specialist agent.
•  W1 Project — E-commerce Operations Agent: severity evaluation, state and ALERT/LOG decisions — the single-agent baseline today's orchestration outgrows.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain orchestration principles; progress from single agent → single agent with tools → multi-agent with an orchestrator → adding a validator/critic; route requests to specialists; and debug multi-agent flows. Evidenced by the multi-agent healthcare/booking system (Coordinator + specialist agents) and the Trip Planner on n8n.

4. What this prepares learners for Orchestration underpins conversational multi-agent systems (W4), workflow integration (W5), and the capstone. The critic/validator pattern is an early form of the verification thinking in the Self-Improving Agents deep dive. Debugging skills feed directly into evaluation and ops (W6).

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback: "One agent decided things last week; now a Coordinator decides which agent acts."
•  Frame the Validator/Critic as reliability engineering — a preview of Week 6 evaluation.
•  Note each specialist is just a Week-1 agent; only the wiring is new.
•  Warn that more agents means more cost, latency, and debugging — a Week 6/7 theme.
•  Tie routing logic to the manager's job of assigning work to the right specialist.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Why not one strong agent instead of many?"
•  "What does the Critic actually add?"
•  "How do I debug when a multi-agent flow goes wrong?"
•  "Doesn't every added agent add cost and latency?"
•  "How do I decide how to split responsibilities?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Orchestration is decomposition by responsibility.
2.  A Validator/Critic is how you buy reliability from unreliable parts.
3.  Each agent is still a simple loop; complexity lives in coordination.
4.  More agents means more cost and failure surface.
5.  Debugging multi-agent flows is a core operational skill.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "More agents = smarter." Clarify the coordination tax.
•  "The critic is optional polish." Clarify it's often what makes the system trustworthy enough to ship.

9. One-minute recap for instructors EMs arrive able to build a grounded single agent. Today they orchestrate teams of agents with a Coordinator and — crucially — a Validator/Critic that catches bad outputs. Emphasize the critic as reliability engineering, not decoration; it's how managers get dependable behavior from non-deterministic components. Reinforce that each specialist is just last week's agent and that the real skill is decomposition and debugging. Flag the cost/latency tax of more agents now, because Weeks 6 and 7 make managers accountable for it. Next week these agents gain a voice and a conversational interface.

Week 4.title: Conversational & Multimodal Agents
Week 4.content:
EM Module 4 (W4) — Conversational & Multimodal Agents

1. Course Journey This module adds the interface layer: voice and conversation, so agents meet users where they are. It exists because many high-value business agents (support, ops assistants) are voice- or chat-first, and managers need to understand the audio stack's tradeoffs (latency, cost, quality). It follows orchestration because a good voice assistant is usually a multi-agent system with a friendly front door.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W3 — Orchestration principles: model cards, single vs multi-agent, orchestration design patterns, and why orchestration matters for risk visibility and control.
•  W3 — The Trip Planner progression: V0 with no agent or tools; V1 a single agent with guardrails and governance; V2 a single agent with a scoped Google Search tool (SerpAPI) and trusted sources, then a Telegram chatbot; V3 specialist agents with diversified models, tools and sub-agents under "one role = one job = one output contract"; V4 a Validator/Critic adding controls, budgeting and enforcement.
•  W3 — Debugging: flow reliability, troubleshooting, observability dashboards, error handling and retry, and modular workflows.
•  W2 — RAG and grounding: chunking, metadata, embeddings, Pinecone, reranking and context injection.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W3 Project — Trip Planner AI Agent (n8n): specialist agents for flights, hotels and activities under an orchestrator that keeps the plan consistent, optimized and aligned with the user's goals.
     Callback: a strong voice assistant is usually this same orchestrator-plus-specialists design with a spoken front door.
•  W3 Assignment — Multi-agent healthcare system (n8n): a Coordinator Agent routes requests to specialists for doctor booking, hospital comparison and emergency assistance, and diagnostic services, over Google Sheets datasets, through a conversational interface.
     Callback: it was already conversational in text — ask what changes when the same user is speaking during an emergency. Latency and error tolerance are today's themes.
•  W2 Project and Assignment — RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent: grounded, cited retrieval over enterprise documents and a vector database.
     Callback: today's Voice AI RAG app is the same retrieval behind a spoken interface.
•  Earlier builds: E-commerce Operations Agent (W1); optional BankCo retention agent (W0).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: describe the 2026 voice-AI frontier; explain the voice pipeline (speech-to-text → reasoning → text-to-speech); build a Streamlit audio bot and an ElevenLabs voice agent; and extend a voice bot into a Voice AI RAG app. Evidenced by the Streamlit Audio Bot and ElevenLabs projects.

4. What this prepares learners for Conversational interfaces recur in the capstone and are a common product surface managers oversee. Latency/cost tradeoffs introduced here feed optimization (W7) and LLMOps. The voice-RAG combination reinforces W2.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Note voice is an interface over the same agent loop — reasoning is unchanged.
•  Tie voice-RAG back to Week 2: "same retrieval, spoken interface."
•  Flag latency as a real UX and cost constraint — a Week 7 theme.
•  Connect the multi-agent voice architecture to Week 3 orchestration.
•  Frame guardrails/best-practice as an early look at Week 6 safety.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How much latency does voice add, and does it break UX?"
•  "Is voice AI fundamentally different or just an interface?"
•  "What does a voice agent cost to run at scale?"
•  "Can I add voice to any of the earlier agents?"
•  "How reliable is voice for real customer interactions?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Multimodality is an interface over the same reasoning loop.
2.  Latency is a first-class UX and cost constraint.
3.  Voice + RAG is a common, powerful business pattern.
4.  Good voice agents are usually orchestrated multi-agent systems.
5.  Guardrails matter more when users interact in real time.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Voice AI is a different kind of AI." Clarify it's the same loop with audio I/O.
•  "Voice is plug-and-play." Clarify latency, cost, and error-handling realities.

9. One-minute recap for instructors EMs arrive able to orchestrate agent teams. Today they add voice and conversation — the interface many business agents actually ship with. Keep the message simple: reasoning doesn't change; the interface does. Anchor the voice-RAG app to Week 2 and stress latency as a real UX and cost constraint they'll be accountable for in Week 7. Note that a strong voice assistant is usually a multi-agent system wearing a friendly front door, linking back to Week 3. Next week agents connect to external tools and each other through standard protocols.

"Is voice AI fundamentally different or just an interface?"
"What does a voice agent cost to run at scale?"

"How reliable is voice for real customer interactions?"

Week 5.title: Agentic Workflow Management (MCP, Agent Skills, A2A)
Week 5.content:
EM Module 5 (W5) — Agentic Workflow Management (MCP, Agent Skills, A2A)

1. Course Journey This module connects agents to the wider world: external tools/data via MCP, reusable Agent Skills, and agent-to-agent (A2A) communication. It exists because production agents rarely live alone — they integrate with systems and negotiate with other agents — and managers must understand these integration standards to plan real deployments. It follows conversational agents because integrated, multi-system workflows are the next scaling step.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W4 — The voice stack: the 2026 "latency war"; the ASR → LLM → TTS flow vs speech-to-speech; the 2026 golden stack; noise and acoustic robustness; notable STT/TTS options; user-experience KPIs and the TTS eval triangle (you cannot optimize everything at once).
•  W4 — Voice in production: audio bots with RAG from basic to enterprise grade, the native multimodal agentic paradigm, a hybrid RAG pattern for voice, WER and utility scoring, a cost formula, a routing brain, and an operational-readiness checklist.
•  W3 — Orchestration: a Coordinator routing to specialists, one role = one job = one output contract, and a Validator/Critic enforcing controls and budgets.
•  W1–W2 — Tools and knowledge: tools wired into a single agent (including the Trip Planner's scoped search tool) and RAG as the knowledge capability.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W4 Projects — Streamlit Audio Bot and ElevenLabs Audio Agent: a speech-in, speech-out bot in Streamlit and a native voice agent in ElevenLabs.
     Callback: ask how many separate integrations these bots needed — MCP is the standard way to stop rebuilding them for every agent.
•  W4 Assignment — Voice AI RAG App: the Streamlit Audio Bot extended into a Voice AI RAG app deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud; optionally, the ElevenLabs agent extended into a personalized voice bot with a multi-agent system connected to channels such as WhatsApp.
     Callback: that optional WhatsApp connection is a hand-wired integration — exactly what MCP standardizes.
•  W3 Project and Assignment — Trip Planner and healthcare system: orchestrator-plus-specialists designs in n8n.
     Callback: today's Travel Weather Comparator stays in the Trip Planner's travel domain — use it as the bridge from orchestration to negotiation.
•  Earlier builds: RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent (W2); E-commerce Operations Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain and use MCP to connect agents to external tools/data; apply Agent Skills as reusable capabilities; implement A2A communication and negotiation; and orchestrate parallel agent interactions. Evidenced by the Travel Weather Comparator (a Coordinator negotiating trade-offs across Weather and Travel agents).

4. What this prepares learners for Integration standards here are assumed in the capstone and echo across the interview deep dives (W12–W13 especially). A2A negotiation directly precedes the Multi-Agent Coordination deep dive. Reusable skills inform how managers think about building maintainable agent platforms.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback: "In Week 1 tools were hand-wired; MCP makes them reusable across agents."
•  Distinguish the two axes: MCP (agent↔tools), A2A (agent↔agents).
•  Tie A2A negotiation to the coordination deep dive later.
•  Frame Agent Skills as reuse — a manager's lever for team efficiency.
•  Connect parallel orchestration to Week 3.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When would I use MCP instead of a direct integration?"
•  "What's the difference between MCP and A2A?"
•  "Are Agent Skills just functions with a nicer name?"
•  "How do agents 'negotiate' — and can I trust the outcome?"
•  "How do these standards affect vendor lock-in?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  MCP standardizes agent-to-tool integration for reuse and portability.
2.  A2A is a different axis — agent-to-agent interaction and negotiation.
3.  Agent Skills are reusable capabilities — a maintainability win.
4.  Integration standards reduce bespoke, brittle work.
5.  Parallel orchestration unlocks real workflow value.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "MCP and A2A are the same." Clarify the two axes.
•  "Standards are enterprise overhead." Clarify they prevent the integration sprawl managers dread.

9. One-minute recap for instructors EMs arrive able to build orchestrated, voice-capable agents. Today they learn the integration standards that let those agents reach external systems (MCP), reuse capabilities (Agent Skills), and coordinate with other agents (A2A). The distinction to protect is the two axes — MCP for tools, A2A for agents — which learners routinely conflate. Frame these standards as the manager's defense against integration sprawl and vendor lock-in. A2A negotiation here previews the coordination deep dive later. Next week the focus shifts from building to evaluating and operating — the manager's home turf.

Week 6.title: Evaluating & Operationalizing AI Agents
Week 6.content:
EM Module 6 (W6) — Evaluating & Operationalizing AI Agents

1. Course Journey This is the EM track's home turf: making agents measurable and operable. It exists because managers are ultimately accountable for whether agent systems work reliably in production, and "it demoed well" is not a metric. It's positioned after learners can build integrated systems, so there's something real to evaluate and operate. This week converts building skills into leadership skills.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W5 — Orchestration and protocols: asynchronous workflows and message graphs; MCP architecture and server primitives; Agent Skills and progressive disclosure; the A2A protocol — design principles, core actors, communication elements and enterprise-ready features — and how Skills, MCP and A2A fit together.
•  W4 — Voice quality metrics: WER, utility scoring, UX KPIs and the TTS eval triangle — their first taste of measuring an AI system.
•  W3 — Validator/Critic and debugging: an in-workflow quality gate plus observability dashboards, error handling and retries — the precursors to formal evaluation.
•  W1–W2 — Foundations: the agent loop and state, RAG, grounding and reranking.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W5 Project — MCP and A2A ecosystem: custom MCP servers and clients, resources, tools and reusable skills for weather intelligence with dynamic tool discovery, extended into an A2A multi-agent system where agents negotiate, resolve conflicts and reach consensus.
     Callback: ask how they would know a negotiated consensus was good — that question is today.
•  W5 Assignment — Travel Weather Comparator: a Travel Agent (flights, hotels, travel times, events) and a Weather Agent, orchestrated in parallel by a Coordinator that negotiates trade-offs and recommends the best destination.
     Callback: "best destination" has no single right answer — a natural case for a golden dataset and an LLM-as-judge.
•  W4 Projects and Assignment — Voice bots and Voice AI RAG App: they already scored voice quality with WER and utility.
     Callback: evaluation isn't new to them; today makes it a lifecycle.
•  W3 Project and Assignment — Trip Planner and healthcare system: orchestrator-plus-specialists designs with a Validator/Critic.
     Callback: the debugging pain there is exactly what traces fix.
•  Earlier builds: RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent (W2); E-commerce Operations Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: run the eval lifecycle (traces, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge); drive continuous agent improvement; and apply AgentOps to operate systems. Evidenced by the Signup Email Agent assignment — analyzing LangSmith traces, expanding a golden dataset with edge cases, building a custom LLM-as-judge, and comparing against a baseline.

4. What this prepares learners for Evaluation and ops are foundational for LLMOps Part 1 & 2 (W6a, W7a), the optimization/fine-tuning economics of W7, the capstone, and the Self-Improving Agents deep dive. This is the measurement discipline the whole back half assumes.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame this as the manager's core competency: "you can't lead what you can't measure."
•  Tie the critic (W3) to formal evaluation here.
•  Connect traces to the debugging pain from Week 3.
•  Preview that Week 7's cost/quality tradeoffs depend on these metrics.
•  Tie golden datasets to the leadership task of defining "good."

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Isn't LLM-as-judge circular?"
•  "How do I build a golden dataset without labeled data?"
•  "What's the difference between observability and evaluation?"
•  "How do I set quality thresholds for a team?"
•  "How continuous should evaluation be?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  You can't improve or lead what you don't measure.
2.  Observability (what happened) and evaluation (was it good) are distinct.
3.  Golden datasets operationalize "good."
4.  LLM-as-judge, done with rubrics, is legitimate.
5.  Continuous evaluation catches drift before users do.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "LLM-as-judge is unreliable." Clarify rubrics/grounding make it robust enough.
•  "Evaluation is a one-time gate." Clarify quality drifts; evaluation is continuous.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is where the EM track turns builders into leaders. EMs arrive able to construct integrated agent systems; today they learn to measure and operate them — the eval lifecycle, golden datasets, LLM-as-judge, and AgentOps. Keep the observability-vs-evaluation distinction sharp and address the LLM-as-judge skepticism directly. Emphasize that defining "good" via golden datasets is a leadership act. These metrics are the currency of every remaining decision: the cost/quality tradeoffs of Week 7, the LLMOps inserts, and the capstone all trade on them. Next comes the economics — model selection, GPU sizing, and when fine-tuning is worth it.

Week 6(a).title: LLMOps Part 1: Operating AI Systems in Production
Week 6(a).content:
EM Module 6(a) — LLMOps Part 1: Operating AI Systems in Production

Shared module — this session uses the SWE Module 8(a) brief. EM-specific notes first, then the full brief.

Track-specific note for EMs: for managers this module is less about the mechanics and more about governance — establishing the Ops mindset, understanding how LLMOps differs from the MLOps/DevOps their teams may already run, and knowing what to ask for (versioned prompts, eval-gated releases, monitoring). Connect it directly to Week 6: the traces, evals, and metrics learners just built are the instruments an ops practice runs on. Emphasize that the manager's job is to institutionalize this discipline, not to implement every piece. See the SWE Module 8(a) brief for the full nine-section treatment; the emphases, misconceptions, and likely questions transfer directly, with the manager reading them as "what should I require of my team?"

What EM learners already know: they arrive from W6's eval lifecycle — the Signup Email Agent project (LangChain with DeepEval offline evals, golden datasets, LangSmith tracing and online evaluation) and its assignment (trace analysis, edge-case golden data, a custom LLM-as-judge and a baseline comparison) — on top of five weeks of builds: the E-commerce Operations Agent (W1); the RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent (W2); the Trip Planner and multi-agent healthcare system (W3); the Streamlit Audio Bot, ElevenLabs agent and Voice AI RAG app (W4); and the MCP/A2A ecosystem and Travel Weather Comparator (W5). They have not built the SWE projects cited in SWE 8(a)'s section 2 (such as the FinTech support system), so translate those callbacks into these examples — the Signup Email Agent is the closest match for an ops practice.

SWE Module 8(a) — LLMOps Part 1: Operating AI Systems in Production

1. Course Journey This short insert exists to give learners the operational vocabulary that Weeks 8 through 9 assume: what "Ops" means, how MLOps evolved, and how LLMOps differs. It sits immediately after observability/evaluation because those are the raw materials of an ops practice. It moves learners toward the capstone by reframing everything they've built as a system to be operated, not just a program to be run.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W8 — Observability: LangSmith setup and tracing, the debugging workflow (wrong answer → open trace → find the fault), and monitoring, tagging and production sampling.
•  W8 — Evaluation: custom evaluators, LLM-as-judge for faithfulness and correctness, MRR, A/B experiments and hill-climbing in LangSmith, and DeepEval/G-Eval wired into CI/CD.
•  W8 — Guardrails and cost: layered guardrails (regex input guard, Moderation API, Presidio PII redaction, Guardrails AI, LLM-based injection detection) and GDPR/HIPAA patterns; token economics with tiktoken, the before/after methodology, semantic caching, audit logging and the cost–quality Pareto frontier.
•  W4–W7 — End-to-end agent systems: LangGraph orchestration, voice and HITL, MCP/ADK/A2A and hybrid retrieval — the kinds of systems an ops practice must run.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System (in progress): a production-grade support system hardened in four passes: observability (traces, runs, run trees, debugging, monitoring, sampling), evaluation (datasets, evaluators, MRR, DeepEval vs LangSmith, G-Eval), guardrails (Regex → Moderation → ML/NER → LLM, Guardrails AI, Presidio, GDPR/HIPAA) and cost (token economics, before/after methodology, four optimization patterns).
     Callback: hold it up as the system an ops practice would run — they already own its instruments.
•  W8 Assignment — Observability, evaluation, guardrails and cost: LangSmith and DeepEval tracing and custom metrics; multi-layer input/output guardrails; token tracking, semantic caching, structured logging, audit trails, budget monitoring and quality regression testing.
•  W7 Project — PubMedQA Hybrid Search: dense-only vs sparse-only vs hybrid (RRF) retrieval in Qdrant.
•  Earlier builds: Real Estate Negotiation and the MCP/ADK/A2A exercises (W6); AxiomCart and SnackStack (W5); Travel Planner and Content Writer (W4); SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: articulate the "Ops mindset" (reliability, repeatability, monitoring, iteration); explain what MLOps established and why; and describe how LLMOps extends and differs from classic MLOps (prompts as artifacts, non-determinism, eval-driven deployment). They leave able to talk about their systems in production/operational terms, grounded by a demo.

4. What this prepares learners for This vocabulary is the frame for W9 fine-tuning (which needs deployment/versioning thinking) and LLMOps Part 2 (W9a). It shapes how learners reason about the capstone as a deployable, maintainable system and underpins the productionization phases in the later deep dives.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Connect to Week 8: "the traces, evals, and cost metrics you just learned are the instruments an ops practice runs on."
•  Contrast with traditional software ops learners may know: "same discipline, new failure modes — non-determinism and prompt drift."
•  Foreshadow Week 9: "you can't fine-tune responsibly without versioning and deployment discipline — that's LLMOps."
•  Note that the capstone's grade partly reflects whether it's built like something operable, not just demo-able.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How is LLMOps different from the DevOps/MLOps I already know?"
•  "Why is non-determinism such a big deal operationally?"
•  "Is a prompt really an 'artifact' I need to version?"
•  "Do I need all this ops machinery for a small project?"
•  "Where does evaluation fit in a deployment pipeline?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Ops is a mindset — reliability, monitoring, iteration — before it's tooling.
2.  LLMOps inherits from MLOps but adds non-determinism and prompt/version management.
3.  Evaluation is part of the deployment loop, not a separate activity.
4.  Prompts, datasets, and eval suites are versioned artifacts.
5.  "It runs" and "it's operable" are different bars.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "LLMOps is just MLOps rebranded." Clarify the genuinely new problems: non-determinism, prompt/version drift, eval-gated releases.
•  "Ops is only for large teams." Clarify the mindset scales down; even a solo project benefits from monitoring and versioned prompts.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is a short framing module: give learners the operational language to describe what they've built. They arrive fluent in building and evaluating agents; today they learn to see those agents as systems that must be deployed, monitored, and iterated — the Ops mindset, MLOps lineage, and what LLMOps adds on top. The one idea to leave them with is that evaluation is part of the release loop, not a final polish. This sets up fine-tuning next week (which demands versioning and deployment discipline) and the capstone's expectation that systems be operable, not just demoable.

Week 7.title: Optimizing and Fine-tuning Agents
Week 7.content:
EM Module 7 (W7) — Optimizing and Fine-tuning Agents

1. Course Journey This module teaches the economics of agent systems — what drives cost, how to select models, size GPUs, and when fine-tuning pays off. It exists because managers own budgets and must make build/buy/tune decisions defensibly. It comes after evaluation because every optimization decision is a tradeoff between cost, latency, and quality that only metrics can adjudicate.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W6 — The eval lifecycle: eval datasets and their sources; offline vs online evals and how they connect; rule-based, reference-based (ROUGE, BLEU, BERTScore), execution-based, LLM-as-judge and human evaluation; evaluation layers.
•  W6 — Continuous improvement and AgentOps: collecting and processing feedback and the dual flywheel with LLM-as-judge; the LLMOps landscape, monitoring tools, guardrails, governance and team operating model, success and failure definitions, and pre-release gates.
•  W6(a) — LLMOps Part 1: the Ops mindset, MLOps vs LLMOps vs AgentOps, seven production failure modes, prompt versioning, model selection and routing, token economics, exact and semantic caching, and a Langfuse-observed travel-agent demo.
•  W2 — RAG as the knowledge lever: grounding via retrieval — the option to rule out before fine-tuning.
•  W4 — Latency and cost: the voice-stack cost formula and latency trade-offs they now generalize.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W6 Project — Signup Email Agent (LangChain): personalized welcome emails with structured outputs, offline evals in DeepEval, golden datasets, LangSmith tracing and online evaluation for production monitoring.
     Callback: its golden dataset is the method they will use today to compare zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuned approaches.
•  W6 Assignment — Signup Email Agent improvement: analyzed LangSmith traces, improved the prompt, added edge cases to the golden dataset, built a custom LLM-as-judge for personalization, and compared results against the baseline.
     Callback: that before/after comparison is exactly how today's optimization decisions get settled.
•  W2 Project and Assignment — RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent: their reference for "better retrieval before fine-tuning."
•  Earlier builds: MCP/A2A ecosystem and Travel Weather Comparator (W5); Streamlit Audio Bot, ElevenLabs agent and Voice AI RAG app (W4); Trip Planner and healthcare system (W3); E-commerce Operations Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: use an optimization frame (cost vs latency vs quality); identify what drives LLM costs; select models appropriately; reason about GPU sizing and deployment; and decide when to fine-tune versus prompt or retrieve. Evidenced by the customer-support ticket classifier assignment — comparing zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned approaches on accuracy, cost, and latency, and writing a total-cost-of-ownership recommendation memo.

4. What this prepares learners for Cost/quality reasoning is decisive in the capstone and central to the optimization and productionization phases of the interview deep dives. The TCO recommendation-memo skill is exactly the managerial artifact the deep dives assume.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the whole module as decision-making: prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune, cheapest sufficient option first.
•  Tie every tradeoff back to Week 6 metrics: "you can only optimize what you measured."
•  Callback to Week 2: "sometimes better retrieval beats fine-tuning."
•  Connect the TCO memo to real budget ownership.
•  Preview that the deep dives make learners defend these tradeoffs live.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When is fine-tuning actually worth the cost?"
•  "How do I estimate total cost of ownership for an agent system?"
•  "Zero-shot vs few-shot vs fine-tuned — how do I choose?"
•  "What's the biggest hidden cost in production agents?"
•  "How do I justify a model choice to leadership?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Every optimization is a cost/latency/quality tradeoff.
2.  Reach for the cheapest sufficient tool (prompt < RAG < fine-tune).
3.  Fine-tuning changes behavior, not knowledge — and it has real TCO.
4.  Model selection and GPU sizing are budget decisions.
5.  A TCO recommendation memo is the manager's deliverable.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Fine-tuning adds knowledge." Clarify: behavior vs knowledge; RAG for facts.
•  "The best model is the biggest one." Clarify that cost/latency often make a smaller model the right call.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This module hands EMs the economics they own: cost drivers, model selection, GPU sizing, and the fine-tune-vs-alternatives decision, expressed as a total-cost-of-ownership memo. Learners arrive able to measure quality (Week 6); today they trade quality against cost and latency. Reinforce the decision hierarchy — cheapest sufficient tool first — and the key distinction that fine-tuning changes behavior, not knowledge. The TCO memo is the deliverable that mirrors their real job. This closes the core curriculum; next is the capstone, then four senior system-design deep dives shared with the SWE track.

Week 7(a).title: LLMOps Part 2: Production Readiness
Week 7(a).content:
EM Module 7(a) — LLMOps Part 2: Production Readiness

Shared module — this session uses the SWE Module 9(a) brief. EM-specific notes first, then the full brief.

Track-specific note for EMs: managers should read this as the production-readiness checklist they hold their teams to — AgentOps, continuous evals, reliability (retries/fallbacks/isolation), and cost at scale. Connect it to Week 6 (the instruments) and Week 7 (the economics). The one idea to leave EMs with is that reliability in a non-deterministic system is a design decision to require and review, not a prompt to tweak. See SWE Module 9(a) for the full brief; the emphases apply directly, read through a governance lens.

What EM learners already know: W7's optimization frame — token economics, KV cache, model selection, GPU sizing and total cost of ownership — from the customer-support ticket classification project (zero-shot, few-shot and LoRA fine-tuning with OpenAI and quantized open-source models) and its assignment (a new feature-request category, re-run comparisons and a TCO recommendation memo); W6's eval lifecycle and the Signup Email Agent; and the 6(a) Ops mindset. Translate SWE 9(a)'s project callbacks: the ticket classifier stands in for the QLoRA pipeline, and the Signup Email Agent for the FinTech system.

SWE Module 9(a) — LLMOps Part 2: Production Readiness

1. Course Journey Part 1 gave the ops mindset; this insert makes it concrete for agents specifically. It exists to consolidate AgentOps, evals, reliability, and cost into a production-readiness checklist right before the capstone. It's positioned here so learners walk into their capstone thinking like operators, not just builders.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W8 — The trust toolkit: tracing and the debugging workflow, evaluators and CI/CD evals, layered guardrails, token tracking, semantic caching and audit logging.
•  W8(a) — LLMOps Part 1: the Ops mindset, the seven production failure modes unique to AI, the AI system lifecycle, prompt versioning, model routing, caching, HITL patterns and Langfuse observability.
•  W9 — Fine-tuning and domain adaptation: the prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune decision framework; full fine-tuning vs PEFT (LoRA, QLoRA, prefix tuning, adapter layers, IA3); QLoRA internals (4-bit NF4, double quantization); dataset sourcing and the chat format; SFTTrainer and hyperparameters; adapter deployment on Hugging Face (adapter toggle, merge decision, four deployment strategies, scale-to-zero); LangSmith evaluation of base vs fine-tuned.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W9 Project — Healthcare QLoRA Fine-Tuning Pipeline (in progress): two controlled QLoRA experiments fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct on a free Colab T4, each up to three epochs, each ending in a documented improvement or a reproducible regression — across strategy and dataset prep, QLoRA training, Hugging Face deploy and inference, and LangSmith evaluation.
     Callback: in class, v1 (ChatDoctor) regressed on all three metrics while v2 (WikiDoc) was mixed — a ready-made case for regression testing and eval-gated releases.
•  W9 Assignment — Fine-tuning analysis: dataset quality audits, prompt engineering vs fine-tuning comparisons, LoRA/hyperparameter and dataset-size trade-offs, generation-parameter tests, base vs fine-tuned comparisons, deployment-cost estimates and custom evaluation metrics.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: the trust toolkit in one build.
     Callback: today's AgentOps checklist is what would take it from hardened demo to production service.
•  W4 Project — Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System: their own multi-agent travel planner.
     Callback: today's demo hardens a prototype travel agent — the same domain as this project and the 8(a) demo — so each production fix maps onto a design they have already built.
•  Earlier builds: PubMedQA hybrid search (W7); Real Estate Negotiation (W6); AxiomCart and SnackStack (W5); Content Writer (W4); SupportDesk-RAG Parts 1–2 (W2–W3); Autonomous IT Support Agent and CRM Lead Qualifier Agent (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: apply AgentOps practices to multi-step agent systems; treat evals & quality as a continuous, gating process; design for reliability (retries, fallbacks, failure isolation) and manage cost at scale. They leave with a mental production-readiness checklist, grounded by a demo.

4. What this prepares learners for Directly de-risks the capstone and defines what "production-ready" means for it. The reliability and cost themes are load-bearing in every advanced deep dive (W12–W15), where productionization is an explicit phase.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Tie together the whole trust arc: "Week 8 gave you the instruments, 8a the mindset, today the checklist."
•  Connect reliability patterns to Week 6's server-failure recovery and self-correction — "same instincts, system-wide now."
•  Frame cost-at-scale as the grown-up version of Week 4's "more agents cost more."
•  Tell them explicitly: "your capstone will be judged partly on these production concerns."

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "What does 'production-ready' actually mean for an agent?"
•  "How do I make a non-deterministic system reliable?"
•  "How often should evals run — every deploy, continuously?"
•  "What's the biggest cost trap in agent systems at scale?"
•  "How is AgentOps different from the LLMOps we just covered?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Reliability for agents means designing for failure — retries, fallbacks, isolation.
2.  Evals are continuous and gating, not one-time.
3.  Cost management is an architectural concern at scale.
4.  AgentOps applies ops discipline to multi-step, non-deterministic systems.
5.  Production readiness is a checklist you can articulate and defend.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "If it passes evals once, it's production-ready." Clarify that quality drifts; evals must run continuously.
•  "Reliability is about better prompts." Clarify it's about system design — fallbacks, retries, graceful degradation.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This short capstone-launch module consolidates the trust arc into production readiness for agents: AgentOps, continuous evals, reliability, and cost at scale. Learners arrive with the instruments (Week 8), the mindset (8a), and fine-tuning experience (Week 9); today they get the checklist that ties it together. Weeks 8–9.title: Project Sessions
Weeks 8–9.content:
EM Capstone — Project Sessions

1. Course Journey The capstone forces EMs to integrate the whole track into one operable, defensible system — and to lead its design decisions. Options include a Multi-Agent BRD-to-Engineering System, an AI-Powered Hiring Intelligence System, a Team Sentiment & Growth Feedback System, or BYOP. It sits here because learners now hold the full toolkit plus the evaluation and cost discipline that distinguishes managerial work.

2. What learners already know The full track — plus a set of builds that anchor each capstone decision.
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1–W7 — The full track: reasoning agents and state (W1), RAG and grounding (W2), orchestration with a Validator/Critic (W3), voice and multimodal agents (W4), MCP, Agent Skills and A2A (W5), the eval lifecycle and AgentOps (W6), and optimization, model selection, GPU sizing and fine-tuning economics (W7).
•  W6(a), W7(a) — LLMOps: the Ops mindset and the production-readiness checklist — AgentOps, continuous evals, reliability and cost at scale — which doubles as a grading lens.
•  Claude Code floater session (if already held for this cohort): spec-driven development vs "vibe coding," the BMAD method and its artifact chain (product brief → PRD → architecture → stories), and CLAUDE.md as project memory — directly relevant to the BRD-to-Engineering option.
Prior builds each capstone option extends
•  Multi-Agent BRD-to-Engineering System: planning, design and validation agents turn unstructured BRDs into engineering-ready outputs, grounded by RAG and refined by a rubric-driven critic loop, with structured outputs, guardrails and observability.
     Builds on: the W3 Validator/Critic and "one role = one job = one output contract," W2 grounding, and W6 golden datasets and LLM-as-judge.
•  AI-Powered Hiring Intelligence System: agents analyze hiring-funnel data — sourcing quality, rejection patterns, panel load and pipeline health — with RAG over historical insights, evaluation of insight quality, and cost/latency/accuracy optimization.
     Builds on: the RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent (W2), W6 evaluation, and the W7 benchmarking and TCO method from the ticket classifier.
•  Multi-Agent Team Sentiment & Growth Feedback System: survey generation through response analysis, insight extraction and action recommendations, with RAG grounding, human-in-the-loop validation, evaluation frameworks, PII anonymization and bias checks.
     Builds on: W2 grounding, the W6 eval lifecycle and guardrails, and the RM-in-the-loop decision support from the optional BankCo exercise (W0).
•  BYOP: any idea — ask each learner to name the two prior builds it extends; if they can't, the scope is probably unanchored.

4. What this prepares learners for The capstone is the concrete case the interview deep dives (W10–W13) abstract from — coordination, verification, research systems, and data-reasoning systems all reuse its decisions.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Force justification of every choice against earlier weeks, especially evaluation and cost.
•  Redirect "make it smarter" toward retrieval and evaluation, not more prompting.
•  Treat production readiness (7a) as a grading lens.

•  Reward restraint and defensible tradeoffs over feature count.

•  "Is BYOP riskier than a guided track?"
•  "How do I show decisions, not just a demo?"
•  "Do I need to use every technique?"
•  "How do I present cost/reliability tradeoffs?"

2.  Cheapest sufficient tool wins.
3.  Evaluation and cost analysis are deliverables.
4.  Reliability and TCO must be explicit.
5.  The decision narrative matters as much as the demo.

•  "More techniques = better." Clarify restraint and rationale win.
•  "The demo is the deliverable." Clarify decisions, evaluation, and operability are.

Week 10.title: Agentic Research Systems
Week 10.content:
EM W10 — Agentic Research Systems

Shared module — this session uses the SWE Module 12 (W12) brief. EM-specific notes first, then the full brief.

EM delta: emphasize scoping, memory/guardrail requirements, and productionization decisions a manager would own; lighter on implementation.

What EM learners already know (use in place of the SWE section 2 lists): builds from W1–W7 — the E-commerce Operations Agent; the RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent; the Trip Planner and multi-agent healthcare system; the Streamlit Audio Bot, ElevenLabs agent and Voice AI RAG app; the MCP/A2A ecosystem and Travel Weather Comparator; the Signup Email Agent (DeepEval, LangSmith, LLM-as-judge); and the LoRA ticket classifier with its TCO memo — plus their capstone (BRD-to-Engineering, Hiring Intelligence, Team Sentiment & Growth Feedback, or BYOP).
