SWE Module 12 (W12) — Agentic Research Systems: Planning, Tools & Guardrails

1. Course Journey This deep dive exists to rehearse designing a research agent — one that plans multi-step investigations, uses tools, remembers, and stays guarded — at interview depth. It comes after the capstone because it presumes learners can already build such systems; now they practice defending the design. It moves them toward the job-search finish line, where system-design fluency, not just working code, is what's assessed.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1 — Planning and the agent loop: ReAct, planning and reasoning, agentic design patterns — today's refresh extends these to Plan-and-Execute, hybrids, Reflexion, Tree of Thoughts and CodeAct.
•  W1, W6 — Tools: function calling and MCP (primitives, transports, multiple servers, automatic tool discovery, failure recovery and LLM self-correction).
•  W2–W3, W7 — Retrieval: embeddings, chunking, indexing, RAG evaluation, and hybrid dense + sparse search with RRF — the research agent's retrieval module.
•  W1, W4 — Memory: short- vs long-term memory, LangGraph checkpointers and the Memory Store.
•  W8, W8(a), W9(a) — Trust and production: tracing, evaluators, LLM-as-judge, layered guardrails including prompt-injection detection, and cost tracking; retries, circuit breakers, fallback chains and graceful degradation.
Projects and assignments already built
•  Capstone (W10–11): their own end-to-end system — the richest source of "I already made this decision" answers.
     Callback: ask each learner to bring one planning, one memory and one guardrail decision from it.
•  W4 Project — Smart Travel Planning Multi-Agent System: answered travel questions with deep research and ran multiple queries in parallel — the closest earlier build to a research agent.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: a traced, evaluated, guarded multi-agent system — their reference for Phase 4 (observability + feedback) and Phase 5 (testing).
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: retrieval and generation metrics plus Agentic RAG — the grounding and citation story behind research-agent guardrails.
•  Also relevant: PubMedQA hybrid search over research abstracts (W7); Real Estate Negotiation over MCP data with A2A (W6).

3. What learners will learn today Working through six phases — fundamentals refresh, system design, memory design, observability + feedback, testing strategy, productionization — learners will be able to: architect a research agent from a blank prompt; justify memory and tool choices; design guardrails and feedback loops; and articulate a productionization path. They leave able to whiteboard a research-agent design end to end.

4. What this prepares learners for This is terminal interview preparation, but it also reinforces patterns reused in Text-to-SQL (W13) and Multi-Agent Coordination (W14) — planning, tool design, and guardrails are shared vocabulary across all three.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Anchor every phase to a capstone decision: "you already made this choice — now say why out loud."
•  Tie memory design to Week 2's short/long-term memory and vector stores.
•  Tie guardrails and feedback to Week 8's observability and evaluation.
•  Frame productionization against LLMOps (W8a/9a).
•  Note that the phase structure itself is a reusable interview framework.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How deep should I go on each phase in a 45-minute interview?"
•  "How do I choose memory architecture on the spot?"
•  "What guardrails do interviewers expect me to mention?"
•  "How is a research agent different from a RAG system?"
•  "What's a strong answer for 'how would you productionize this'?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  System design is a structured conversation — the phases are a framework, not a script.
2.  Every choice needs a stated tradeoff.
3.  Memory and guardrails are where weak candidates go silent — over-prepare them.
4.  Feedback loops distinguish a toy from a system.
5.  Productionization thinking signals seniority.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "System design is about naming tools." Clarify it's about justified tradeoffs and failure handling.
•  "A research agent is just RAG." Clarify it adds planning, multi-step tool use, and iterative refinement.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Learners arrive able to build research agents; this session makes them able to defend the design under interview pressure. Walk the six phases as a reusable framework and force a stated tradeoff at every step, especially on memory and guardrails, where candidates typically stall. Anchor everything to concrete capstone decisions so it's recall, not invention. The goal isn't new capability — it's fluency and structure. This is the first of four interview rehearsals; the planning/tools/guardrails vocabulary here recurs across the next three.

SWE Module 13 (W13) — Agentic Text-to-SQL: Reliable Data Reasoning Systems

1. Course Journey This deep dive tackles one of the hardest, most-asked interview problems: an agent that turns natural language into reliable SQL over real schemas. It exists because Text-to-SQL concentrates almost every course theme — retrieval (schema), sub-agents, tool design, guardrails, self-correction, evaluation — into one high-stakes problem where being wrong is worse than being silent. It comes late because it assumes command of all those pieces.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W7 — Hybrid retrieval: sparse (inverted index, SPLADE) and dense vectors fused with RRF — today's schema retrieval combines BM25 and dense embeddings with other signals in a five-signal funnel.
•  W4 — Sub-agents and LangGraph state machines: routing, sub-agents and when not to use them — the basis for today's sub-agent topology and self-correction state machine.
•  W6 — MCP and self-correction: MCP servers and tool contracts, server-failure recovery and LLM self-correction — today's execute_sql tool sits behind read-only and read-write MCP servers.
•  W8 — Guardrails, evaluation and cost: layered guardrails and injection defense, LLM-as-judge, CI/CD evals and cost tracking.
•  W12 — Deep dive: Agentic Research Systems: the phased interview framework; ReAct vs Plan-and-Execute; tool failure modes; layered prompt-injection defense; memory trade-offs; the limits of LLM-as-judge; and productionization (invocation patterns, circuit breakers, caching).
Projects and assignments already built
•  W12 — Market Research Report Generator (whiteboard design): designed last week, from requirements through productionization.
     Callback: today repeats that cadence — requirements, architecture, failure modes, guardrails, evaluation, production — under a much stricter reliability bar.
•  W7 Project — PubMedQA Hybrid Search: hands-on proof that lexical plus semantic retrieval beats either alone.
     Callback: table and column names behave like the exact identifiers sparse vectors caught in that project.
•  Capstone — Multi-Agent Customer Support Assistant (if chosen): supervisor-routed agents answering over a live relational database with anti-hallucination grounding — learners who built it have already met today's problem at small scale.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: layered guardrails and custom evaluators — the base for today's AST validator, policy-as-code checks and CI eval gate.
•  W6 Assignment — MCP exercises: multi-server tool discovery, server-failure recovery and LLM self-correction — the base for today's retry decision tree.

3. What learners will learn today Across nine phases (framing, pipeline & cost math, schema retrieval, semantic layer & sub-agent topology, tool design, guardrails, self-correction & retry, evaluation & observability, productionization at scale), learners will be able to: design a Text-to-SQL system that retrieves the right schema, decomposes work across sub-agents, guards against unsafe/incorrect queries, self-corrects on failure, and is evaluated and cost-modeled. They leave able to defend a production-grade data-reasoning system.

4. What this prepares learners for Terminal interview prep. It also crystallizes the self-correction/retry pattern that the Self-Improving Agents deep dive (W15) generalizes, and the schema retrieval pattern that reuses hybrid search from W7.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Tie schema retrieval directly to Week 7 hybrid search: "exact table/column names are a lexical-match problem."
•  Connect sub-agent topology to Week 4 orchestration.
•  Tie guardrails to Week 8 and to the cost of a wrong query executing against production data.
•  Connect self-correction to Week 6's LLM self-correction patterns.
•  Frame the cost math phase against LLMOps cost thinking.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Why is Text-to-SQL so much harder than normal RAG?"
•  "How does the agent retrieve the right schema without loading the whole database?"
•  "What guardrails stop a destructive or wrong query?"
•  "How does self-correction work when the SQL fails?"
•  "How do I evaluate correctness when there are many valid queries?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Reliability is the whole game — a confidently wrong query is the worst outcome.
2.  Schema retrieval is a retrieval problem (and hybrid search shines here).
3.  Sub-agent decomposition tames complexity.
4.  Self-correction/retry turns failures into recoveries.
5.  Correctness evaluation is subtle — multiple valid answers exist.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Text-to-SQL is just prompting the model with the schema." Clarify why schema retrieval, guardrails, and self-correction are essential at real scale.
•  "If the SQL runs, it's correct." Clarify that executable and correct are different — evaluation must check semantics.

9. One-minute recap for instructors Text-to-SQL is the course's capstone problem in miniature — retrieval, sub-agents, guardrails, self-correction, evaluation, and cost, all under a strict reliability bar. Learners arrive with every piece; today they assemble and defend them for a problem where being wrong beats being silent only in the sense that both are failures. Anchor schema retrieval to Week 7 hybrid search and self-correction to Week 6. The nine phases are dense — prioritize framing, schema retrieval, guardrails, and self-correction if time is short. Emphasize that reliability, not cleverness, is what interviewers probe. Next up: coordinating many agents.

SWE Module 14 (W14) — Multi-Agent Systems: Coordination & Shared Intelligence

1. Course Journey Week 4 taught learners to build multi-agent systems; this deep dive teaches them to reason rigorously about coordination — roles, contracts, topology, shared state, and the failure modes that emerge when agents depend on each other. It exists because "add more agents" is where naive designs break, and interviewers probe exactly that. It comes late because it presumes fluency with orchestration, MCP/A2A, and reliability.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W4 — LangGraph multi-agent systems: State, persistence, the Memory Store, supervisor/router patterns, sub-agents and when not to use them.
•  W5 — Sub-graphs and HITL: composing sub-graphs and pausing on interrupts for human approval — the seed of today's "HITL on every destructive action."
•  W6 — A2A and Google ADK: Agent Cards, context threading, parts and artifacts; Sequential, Parallel and Loop agents, Agent-as-Tool and callbacks; negotiation orchestration under information asymmetry.
•  W8, W9(a) — Reliability, cost and evaluation: retries, timeouts and circuit breakers, fallback chains, graceful degradation, rate limiting and budget caps; per-agent tracing and routing-accuracy evaluators.
•  W12–W13 — Deep dives 1–2: the eight-stage interview framework (restate, requirements, topology, tools, failure modes, eval, scaling, trade-offs); Plan-and-Execute vs ReAct; sub-agent topology and model selection; self-consistency; six-layer defense in depth.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W4 builds — Travel Planner and Multi-Agent Content Writer: their first supervisor/router designs, with parallel queries and checkpointer memory.
     Callback: ask what each specialist was allowed to read and write — today turns that implicit agreement into typed role contracts and a permission matrix.
•  W5 Project — AxiomCart: an orchestrator routing to a Product Agent sub-graph and a Support Agent, joined by a synthesizer, with HITL — a concrete supervisor, join and human gate.
•  W6 Project — Real Estate Negotiation Workshop: Buyer and Seller agents under an ADK negotiation orchestrator over A2A; the W6 exercises added negotiation-stall detection, hierarchical delegation and shared memory.
     Callback: stall detection is a termination guarantee — the fourth of today's coordination primitives.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: per-agent tracing plus routing_accuracy and keyword_correctness evaluators — the starting point for today's multi-agent evaluation view.
•  Capstone: several tracks are multi-agent (Finnie's six agents, the Customer Support supervisor, ContentAlchemy, SmartDesk).
     Callback: ask learners to redraw theirs using today's four coordination primitives.

3. What learners will learn today Across its phases (clarify, architecture, coordination via agent roles & contracts, coordination topology, shared intelligence, reliability/execution, coordination failure modes, scale, production concerns, tradeoffs), learners will be able to: define agent roles and contracts; choose a coordination topology; design shared intelligence/state; and anticipate and mitigate coordination failure modes at scale. They leave able to defend a multi-agent architecture — including where it shouldn't be multi-agent.

4. What this prepares learners for Terminal interview prep. Consolidates the multi-agent thread that began at W4 and ran through A2A (W6), and pairs with Self-Improving Agents (W15) as the two "advanced systems" interviews.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback to Week 4: "you built these; now define the contracts between them."
•  Tie A2A negotiation (W6) to formal coordination topology here.
•  Connect failure modes to Week 8/9a reliability.
•  Repeatedly ask "would a single agent be simpler?" — the strongest answers know when not to go multi-agent.
•  Frame shared intelligence as the grown-up version of LangGraph state.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When is multi-agent genuinely better than one strong agent?"
•  "What's an 'agent contract' and why does it matter?"
•  "How do coordination failures actually happen?"
•  "How do agents share state reliably at scale?"
•  "How do I discuss tradeoffs without sounding hand-wavy?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Coordination needs explicit roles and contracts, not vibes.
2.  Topology is a design choice with real consequences.
3.  Multi-agent systems fail in new ways — plan for coordination failure.
4.  Knowing when not to use multi-agent is a seniority signal.
5.  Shared intelligence is disciplined shared state.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Multi-agent is always more capable." Clarify the coordination tax and failure surface; sometimes one agent wins.
•  "Agents coordinate automatically." Clarify that contracts, topology, and shared state are deliberately engineered.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is the rigorous sequel to Week 4. Learners can already wire agents together; today they reason about roles, contracts, topology, shared intelligence, and — the part interviews love — coordination failure modes. The single most valuable habit to instill is asking "would one agent be simpler?" before defending a multi-agent design; candidates who default to more agents look junior. Anchor to Week 4 state and Week 6 A2A. Emphasize that multi-agent systems fail in ways single agents don't, and that anticipating those failures is what separates a strong answer from a feature list. One deep dive remains: agents that evaluate and improve themselves.

SWE Module 15 (W15) — Self-Improving Agents: Evaluation & Verification Loops

1. Course Journey The final deep dive closes the loop the whole course has been building toward: agents that verify their own work and improve. Using a code-review system as the anchor, it generalizes evaluation (W3, W8) into verification loops, LLM-as-judge, and online/offline feedback. It exists because self-verification is the frontier of reliable agentic systems and a favorite hard interview topic. It's last because it requires mastery of evaluation, reliability, and multi-agent design.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W3, W8 — Evaluation: Precision/Recall/F1, groundedness, LLM-as-judge (faithfulness, correctness), custom evaluators, MRR, A/B experiments and hill-climbing, DeepEval/G-Eval in CI/CD.
•  W9 — Before/after evaluation: base vs fine-tuned comparisons with LangSmith evaluators for helpfulness, accuracy and safety — including a real regression.
•  W9(a) — Continuous evals: task- vs system-level evaluation, automated vs human review, regression testing in CI/CD, golden and synthetic datasets, and the trust scorecard.
•  W13 — Verification in miniature: AST validation, dry-run/EXPLAIN, self-consistency (choosing K), monthly LLM-judge calibration and CI eval gates.
•  W14 — Coordination: role contracts, supervisor topology, typed shared state and the Critic as an online judge — today's "reviewers as a multi-agent system" builds directly on it.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W14 — Personal Task Execution System (PTES) design: five agents (Planner, Researcher, Decision, Executor, Critic) under a supervisor, with a permission matrix and HITL on destructive actions.
     Callback: PTES's Critic is today's verification loop in embryo.
•  W9 Project — Healthcare QLoRA Fine-Tuning Pipeline: controlled experiments that had to end in a documented improvement or a reproducible regression; in class, v1 (ChatDoctor) regressed on all three metrics.
     Callback: a real case of why verification beats impressions.
•  W8 Project — Multi-Agent FinTech Support System: custom evaluators (routing_accuracy, keyword_correctness), LLM-as-judge for faithfulness and correctness, and DeepEval in CI — the offline-evaluation half of today's design.
•  W3 Project — SupportDesk-RAG Part 2: where "measure, then improve" started; today's golden dataset and per-category precision/recall are the same ideas at production scale.
•  Capstone: each learner's own evaluation and observability plan.
     Callback: ask what theirs caught — and what it missed.

3. What learners will learn today Across its phases (clarify, architecture, context & grounding, the reviewers, signal fusion, why verification is hard, offline evaluation, the verification loop, verifying correctness, LLM-as-judge, online evaluation & feedback, reliability & scale, tradeoffs), learners will be able to: design multiple reviewer agents, fuse their signals, build offline and online verification loops, use LLM-as-judge responsibly, and reason about why verification is genuinely hard. They leave able to defend a self-improving agent architecture.

4. What this prepares learners for Terminal interview prep and the conceptual summit of the program — it ties evaluation, multi-agent design, and reliability into one system. Nothing depends on it downstream; it's the capstone of the interview sequence.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame it as the natural end of the evaluation thread from Week 3 and Week 8.
•  Tie multiple reviewers + signal fusion to Week 14 coordination.
•  Revisit the LLM-as-judge skepticism from Week 8 and resolve it with rubric/grounding techniques.
•  Connect online feedback to LLMOps continuous-eval thinking.
•  Emphasize honesty about verification's limits — a mature, senior stance.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How can an agent reliably judge its own output?"
•  "Isn't LLM-as-judge circular — again?"
•  "What's the difference between offline and online evaluation here?"
•  "Why is verification harder than generation?"
•  "How do I fuse disagreeing reviewer signals?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Verification is harder than generation — respect that difficulty.
2.  Multiple reviewers plus signal fusion beat a single judge.
3.  Grounding and rubrics make LLM-as-judge defensible.
4.  Offline and online evaluation play different roles.
5.  Self-improvement is a loop: verify, learn, iterate.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "An agent can just check its own work." Clarify why naive self-checking fails and why grounded, multi-signal verification is needed.
•  "LLM-as-judge is unreliable, full stop." Clarify that with rubrics, grounding, and multiple judges it's a legitimate, widely-used technique.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is the program's conceptual summit: agents that verify and improve themselves. Learners arrive fluent in evaluation, multi-agent design, and reliability; today those threads converge into verification loops, multiple reviewers with signal fusion, LLM-as-judge done responsibly, and honest treatment of why verification is hard. Resolve the recurring LLM-as-judge skepticism decisively here. The senior stance to leave them with is intellectual honesty about verification's limits paired with concrete techniques to push past them. This completes the interview sequence — from here, learners are rehearsing, not learning. Send them out able to defend the hardest system in the course.

Week 0 (self-paced).title: Foundational Material & Pre-Program Foundations (self-paced orientation)
Week 0 (self-paced).content:
PM Module 0 — Foundational Material & Pre-Program Foundations (self-paced orientation)

Prerequisite scaffolding.

What it covers: a Python crash course plus "Python for Generative AI," and an optional AI exercise. The aim is fluency in reading and reasoning about AI systems, not shipping code.

Why it matters to you as an instructor: PMs need enough technical literacy to earn credibility with engineers and to reason about tradeoffs — not to build production systems. Set that expectation explicitly. The payoff shows up in Week 5 (AI Product Architecture) and the interview phase, where fluency in system vocabulary separates strong PM candidates from hand-wavers. Frame Python here as technical literacy for product judgment.

Week 1.title: Agentic AI Fundamentals (Reflex → Reasoning)
Week 1.content:
PM Module 1 (W1) — Agentic AI Fundamentals (Reflex → Reasoning)

1. Course Journey This module establishes what an agent actually is, so PMs can spec, scope, and evaluate agentic products rather than repeat buzzwords. It exists because product decisions about AI start with understanding the primitive — a reasoning loop that decides and acts. It's first because every later product question (RAG vs agents, cost, evaluation) presumes this foundation.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  Module 0 — Python crash course and Python for Generative AI (self-paced): variables, data types, strings, conditionals, loops and functions; NumPy, Pandas and Matplotlib — enough to read and reason about AI systems and earn credibility with engineers, not to ship code.
•  Pre-class primers for today: Prompting, Introduction to Agents, and LLM client libraries. Assume these were skimmed, not mastered.
•  Product familiarity with AI features: PMs know AI as a product surface and often know automation tools, but few have built the reasoning loop underneath.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W0 Optional AI Exercise — BankCo churn agent (Zapier): acting as an AI PM, learners designed a no-code agent for Relationship Managers: a multi-tab Google Sheet as the source of truth (spend patterns, lounge usage, NPS), at-risk signal detection, a strict Offer Policy, personalized RM-ready email drafts, and a human-in-the-loop workflow that notifies RMs before renewal. Its solution walkthrough is part of this week's topic list.
     Callback: it already used Zapier and a human-in-the-loop step — ask which parts were fixed rules and which needed judgment. The exercise was optional, so expect a mixed room; for many PMs today is their first agent build.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain generative AI and LLMs and their limits; write deliberate prompts; distinguish reflex/rule-based automation from reasoning agents; and build an agent (in Zapier) that triages events, maintains state, and emits a structured decision. Evidenced by the Checkout Incident Detection Agent and the E-Commerce Customer Support project.

4. What this prepares learners for The agent concept underpins RAG (W2), orchestration (W3), and especially AI Product Architecture (W5), where PMs decide whether a problem even needs an agent. It's the base vocabulary for the entire interview phase.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the reflex→reasoning jump as the difference between the automation PMs know and the agents they'll spec.
•  Plant the hallucination pain now — it motivates RAG (W2), evaluation (W6), and governance (W12).
•  Preview Week 5: "the sharpest PM skill is knowing when not to build an agent."
•  Tie state management to reliable product behavior.
•  Keep the tool (Zapier) subordinate to the concept.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How is an agent different from automation we already ship?"
•  "As a PM, how much of this do I build vs spec?"
•  "When is an agent overkill for a feature?"
•  "How do I write requirements for a non-deterministic system?"
•  "How do I evaluate an agent feature's quality?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  An agent is a reasoning loop — a real category beyond automation.
2.  Knowing when an agent is warranted is a core PM skill.
3.  LLM limitations shape what's shippable.
4.  State and structured outputs make agents dependable product components.
5.  Concepts transfer; the no-code tool is incidental.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Agents are just smarter automation." Clarify the reasoning/autonomy shift.
•  "AI features are unpredictable, so specs don't apply." Clarify that evaluation and guardrails make them specifiable.

9. One-minute recap for instructors PMs arrive fluent in products but often fuzzy on what an agent is. Today they build one and learn to see the reasoning loop beneath the hype, so they can spec and scope agentic features credibly. Keep them on concepts, not Zapier mechanics, and make sure they can articulate when an agent is warranted versus overkill — the seed of Week 5's product-architecture judgment. Plant the hallucination pain deliberately; it motivates RAG, evaluation, and governance later. Everything ahead builds on this primitive.

Week 2.title: RAG Knowledge Agents
Week 2.content:
PM Module 2 (W2) — RAG Knowledge Agents

1. Course Journey This module gives agents grounded knowledge and gives PMs the vocabulary to reason about the most common AI-product pattern: retrieval over a private corpus. It exists because "grounded, cite-able answers" is a product requirement PMs constantly negotiate, and they must understand retrieval's parts to scope and evaluate it. It follows the agent loop because grounding is the first major capability upgrade.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1 — Gen AI and LLM fundamentals: rule-based systems to generative AI, use cases, LLMs, prompt engineering and its types, and the limitations of LLMs — hallucination above all.
•  W1 — Agents: agents with tools, how agents solve problems, the evolution of agents, how PMs and TPMs can leverage agents, and two design patterns: reflection and routing.
•  W1 — No-code agent building: the Zapier interface and integrations, tool-based actions over Google Sheets, on-demand and scheduled triggers, and system prompts that set tone.
•  W1 — Post-class reading: LLM limitations → RAG motivation, LLM hallucinations, a bird's-eye view of Transformers, tools + memory + planning + ReAct, LangChain and OpenAI function calling.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W1 Assignment — Checkout Incident Detection Agent (Zapier): monitors new checkout events in Google Sheets, evaluates severity against baseline metrics, applies business rules to triage payment and high-value failures, keeps state to avoid duplicates, writes one ALERT or LOG decision per run and fires a webhook with a JSON payload.
     Callback: it reasoned only about the event in front of it — ask what it would need to cite a policy or a past incident. That's retrieval.
•  W1 Project — E-Commerce Customer Support (Zapier): ingests customer feedback from Google Sheets, labels sentiment NEGATIVE, POSITIVE or NEUTRAL, and drafts professional, empathetic email replies using spreadsheet read and update actions.
     Callback: an ungrounded support reply is where hallucinations reach customers — a natural bridge to grounded, cited answers.
•  W0 Optional AI Exercise — BankCo churn agent: Offer Policy-constrained recommendations with an RM in the loop.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain RAG and why it beats keyword search; reason about chunking and metadata design; understand embeddings and vector databases conceptually; ensure grounded, cited responses; and build a RAG agent. Evidenced by the AI Finance Reporting Agent (retrieve from a vector DB, blend internal/external data, email a report).

4. What this prepares learners for RAG is a central option in the AI Product Architecture decision (W5), a thing to evaluate (W6), and a recurring case in the interview phase (System Design, Production LLMOps). The RAG-vs-fine-tune question returns in W7.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback: "the agent hallucinated with no source — RAG is the product fix."
•  Keep embeddings-vs-vector-DB crisp.
•  Note grounding and citations are product-quality levers PMs can require.
•  Preview Week 5: "RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines is the architecture decision."
•  Tie chunking/metadata to answer quality they'll measure in Week 6.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Embedding vs vector database — what's the difference?"
•  "How do I know if our RAG feature is good enough to ship?"
•  "Does RAG replace fine-tuning?"
•  "Why not just use a bigger context window?"
•  "How do citations affect user trust?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  RAG grounds answers — the main defense against hallucination.
2.  Embeddings encode meaning; vector databases store/search them.
3.  Chunking and metadata quietly govern quality.
4.  Grounding and citations are product-trust levers.
5.  Retrieval quality is measurable and specifiable.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Embeddings and vector databases are the same." Clarify explicitly.
•  "RAG and fine-tuning compete." Clarify: knowledge vs behavior.

9. One-minute recap for instructors PMs arrive having felt hallucination in their first agent. Today they learn RAG well enough to scope, require, and evaluate it — the pattern behind most AI knowledge features. Keep the embeddings-vs-vector-DB distinction sharp and frame grounding and citations as product-trust levers they can demand. Flag that "RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines" is the central decision they'll formalize in Week 5. They leave able to reason about a RAG feature end to end. Next: multiple agents coordinating, with a critic for reliability.

Week 3.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
Week 3.content:
PM Module 3 (W3) — Multi-Agent Orchestration

1. Course Journey This module scales to coordinated agent teams — Planner, Analyzer, Critic — so PMs can reason about decision-support products that decompose work and challenge their own assumptions. It exists because many high-value PM-facing products (prioritization copilots, decision assistants) are multi-agent, and the Critic pattern is how they earn trust. It follows RAG because specialists often need grounded knowledge.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W2 — RAG foundations: types of agents, knowledge agents and their components, what RAG is, when to use it, why it matters for PMs/TPMs, and the components of a RAG pipeline.
•  W2 — Chunking, embeddings and vector databases: recursive and structure-aware chunking, overlap, chunk size and top-k, metadata design; query vs document embeddings, limitations and cost/latency trade-offs; the vector-DB mental model, Pinecone, and top-k plus metadata filtering (precision vs recall vs cost) — each with PM and TPM lenses.
•  W2 — Grounding: what makes an answer trustworthy, why retrieval alone isn't enough, context injection, a response contract users can verify, and safe handling of gaps, weak evidence and conflicts.
•  W1 — The agent loop: reflex vs reasoning, state, structured decisions, and the reflection and routing patterns.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W2 Project — RAG Intelligence Agent (n8n): ingests enterprise documents, embeds them and retrieves semantically to answer leadership questions with grounded, citation-backed insights and trustworthy metrics reports.
     Callback: retrieve → analyze → explain → report is several roles in one flow — today splits roles like these across a Planner, an Analyzer and a Critic.
•  W2 Assignment — AI Finance Reporting Agent: blends internal product performance data from a vector database with external market intelligence and emails a leadership-ready monthly report.
•  W1 Assignment and Project — Checkout Incident Detection Agent and E-Commerce Customer Support (Zapier): their single-agent baselines.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: explain single vs multi-agent tradeoffs; apply core multi-agent patterns; and build a Planner/Analyzer/Critic workflow in LangFlow that evaluates options, challenges assumptions, and supports structured decisions — while reasoning about cost, latency, and debugging. Evidenced by the multi-agent feature-prioritization system and the decision copilot.

4. What this prepares learners for Orchestration and the Critic pattern feed AI Product Architecture (W5), evaluation (W6), the capstone, and the System Design and Governance interview modules. The "when to go multi-agent" judgment is a recurring interview theme.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Callback: "one agent decided things; now a Planner routes and a Critic checks."
•  Frame the Critic as reliability engineering and a preview of evaluation (W6) and governance (W12).
•  Warn that more agents means more cost/latency — a Week 5/6 product tradeoff.
•  Tie decomposition to how PMs already break down problems.
•  Preview that "single vs multi-agent" is a classic interview question.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "Why not one strong agent instead of many?"
•  "What does the Critic add for a product?"
•  "How do cost and latency scale with more agents?"
•  "How do I spec a multi-agent feature?"
•  "How do I debug a multi-agent flow as a PM?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Orchestration is decomposition by responsibility.
2.  A Critic buys reliability — often what makes a feature shippable.
3.  Each agent is still a simple loop; complexity is coordination.
4.  More agents means more cost, latency, and failure surface.
5.  Knowing when not to go multi-agent is a PM strength.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "More agents = smarter product." Clarify the coordination tax.
•  "The Critic is optional." Clarify it's often the trust mechanism.

9. One-minute recap for instructors PMs arrive able to reason about a grounded single agent. Today they orchestrate Planner/Analyzer/Critic teams — the shape of many decision-support products — and, importantly, learn when not to. Frame the Critic as the trust mechanism and flag the cost/latency tax they'll weigh in Weeks 5 and 6. Tie decomposition to skills they already have as PMs. "Single vs multi-agent" is a classic interview question, so make the tradeoff reasoning explicit. Next: conversational and voice agents as product surfaces.

Week 4.title: Multi-modal & Conversational Agents
Week 4.content:
PM Module 4 (W4) — Multi-modal & Conversational Agents

1. Course Journey This module adds voice and conversation as product surfaces and teaches the architecture and guardrails behind them. It exists because conversational AI is a major product category and PMs must reason about its UX, reliability, and guardrail tradeoffs. It follows orchestration because good conversational products are usually multi-agent underneath.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W3 — Single vs multi-agent: the evolution of AI systems, the anatomy of an agent, generative vs agentic AI, the spectrum of autonomy, and when one agent stops being enough.
•  W3 — Core multi-agent patterns: sequential chaining, parallel lenses plus merge, the critic loop as a quality gate, hierarchical orchestration, and the router/dispatcher.
•  W3 — Cost, latency and debugging: predicting call explosion, setting limits and budgets, and multi-agent do's and don'ts.
•  W2 — RAG: grounding, citations and a verifiable response contract.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W3 Project — Multi-agent decision copilot (LangFlow): turns a product decision brief into a decision memo: Planner and Researcher in sequence, two Analyzers (Customer/Growth and Risk/Reliability), a Synthesis agent that resolves disagreements, Critic and Reviser agents, a Confidence Scorer and a Publisher that formats for Notion.
     Callback: today's Greeter is their router/dispatcher pattern with a conversational front door.
•  W3 Assignment — Feature prioritization system (LangFlow): Planner, Analyzer and Critic agents evaluate feature requests, recommend, challenge assumptions and support structured decisions.
•  W2 Project and Assignment — RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent: grounded retrieval — today's specialists answer from scoped knowledge bases the same way.
•  Earlier builds: Checkout Incident Detection Agent and E-Commerce Customer Support (W1); optional BankCo churn agent (W0).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: reason about multi-modal agents; understand the conversational architecture (greeter + specialist analysts); apply guardrails and best practices; and build a voice product. Evidenced by the Product Launch Command Center (ElevenLabs) and the TaskFlow Product Health Monitor (voice queries over feedback, tickets, and metrics via a Greeter + specialist analysts).

4. What this prepares learners for Conversational architecture and guardrails feed AI Product Architecture (W5), evaluation (W6), and the UX & Trust portion of the Product Sense interview module. Guardrails preview Governance (W12).

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Note voice is an interface over the same reasoning loop.
•  Tie the Greeter+analysts pattern to Week 3 orchestration.
•  Frame guardrails as trust and a preview of Week 12 governance.
•  Flag latency as a UX and cost tradeoff (Week 6).
•  Connect voice-over-data to Week 2 RAG.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When is voice the right surface vs chat or dashboard?"
•  "How much latency is acceptable in a voice product?"
•  "What guardrails do conversational products need?"
•  "Is voice AI a different technology or just an interface?"
•  "How do I measure conversational quality?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Multimodality is an interface decision over the same loop.
2.  Conversational products are usually orchestrated multi-agent systems.
3.  Guardrails are trust infrastructure.
4.  Latency is a UX and cost tradeoff.
5.  Voice-over-data (RAG) is a powerful product pattern.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Voice AI is fundamentally different." Clarify it's the same loop with audio I/O.
•  "Guardrails are just profanity filters." Clarify they cover format, PII, and business rules.

9. One-minute recap for instructors PMs arrive able to orchestrate agent teams. Today they treat voice and conversation as product surfaces — with architecture (Greeter + specialists) and guardrails as first-class concerns. Keep the message that reasoning doesn't change; the interface and trust layer do. Tie the architecture to Week 3 and frame guardrails as a preview of Week 12 governance. Stress latency as a real UX and cost tradeoff. Next is the track's pivot: AI Product Architecture, where PMs learn to choose between RAG, agents, and pipelines.

Week 5.title: AI Product Architecture
Week 5.content:
PM Module 5 (W5) — AI Product Architecture

1. Course Journey This is the PM track's intellectual center: system design in agentic terms and the decisive RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines judgment. It exists because the highest-leverage PM skill isn't building — it's choosing the right architecture for a problem and defending the tradeoffs. It's positioned after PMs have seen all three patterns in action, so the comparison is grounded in experience rather than abstraction.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W4 — Multi-modal and voice agents: what makes an agent multi-modal, the PM/TPM "human switchboard" bottleneck, and the limits of chained STT + TTS vs speech-to-speech in ElevenLabs.
•  W4 — Conversational architecture: a 5-node, 12-edge workflow: a Greeter that routes intent, specialist nodes with scoped knowledge bases, forward and backward edges for re-routing, and global vs subagent prompts — plus why multi-agent (attention, leakage, modularity).
•  W4 — Guardrails and best practices: guardrails at global-prompt and subagent levels, multi-agent design principles, and voice-design do's and don'ts.
•  W3 — Patterns and their cost: sequential, parallel, critic-loop, hierarchical and router patterns, and the call-explosion math.
•  W1–W2 — Agents vs automation, and RAG: reflex vs reasoning, and grounded, cited answers over a private corpus.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W4 Project — Product Launch Command Center (ElevenLabs): one number for stakeholders, routed by intent to Technical Readiness, GTM & Marketing or Executive Briefing specialists, built in the Workflow Canvas with knowledge-base files, global and subagent prompts, and forward/backward edges.
     Callback: ask which parts truly needed an agent and which could have been a pipeline or a simple FAQ — that is today's decision.
•  W4 Assignment — TaskFlow Product Health Monitor (ElevenLabs): a Greeter plus three analyst agents with scoped knowledge bases answering voice questions on NPS, app reviews, ticket trends, churn risk, engagement and conversion funnels, with cross-routing mid-conversation.
•  W3 Project and Assignment — Decision copilot and feature prioritization system (LangFlow): their reference point for the "Agents" option.
•  W2 Project and Assignment — RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent: their reference point for the "RAG" option.
•  W1 Assignment — Checkout Incident Detection Agent: a rule-heavy triage flow — a good "pipeline or agent?" discussion case.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: think in agentic system-design terms (control, execution, reliability); reason about AI decision-making; apply design patterns and their tradeoffs; and — centrally — decide when to use RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines. Evidenced by the Slack Project Status Chatbot and the Multi-Agent Daily Digest (orchestration, guardrails, state, synthesis, error handling, graceful degradation).

4. What this prepares learners for This is the backbone of the interview phase: Agentic System Design (W11) is a direct extension, and Product Sense (W10) leans on the AI-vs-non-AI and architecture-choice reasoning. Design-pattern and tradeoff fluency recurs in Governance (W12) and Production LLMOps (W13).

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the whole module as choosing, tying each option to the week it was learned (RAG=W2, Agents=W3, Pipelines=automation instincts).
•  Callback to Week 1: "sometimes the answer is a pipeline, not an agent."
•  Connect control/execution/reliability to guardrails (W4) and to Week 12 governance.
•  Preview that Week 11's layered system design builds on this.
•  Emphasize graceful degradation as a product-reliability concept.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How do I decide between RAG, an agent, and a plain pipeline?"
•  "When is AI the wrong answer entirely?"
•  "What does 'graceful degradation' mean for an AI product?"
•  "How do I defend an architecture choice to engineers?"
•  "Aren't agents always the most impressive option?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Architecture choice is the PM's highest-leverage AI skill.
2.  RAG, Agents, and Pipelines solve different problems — match to the need.
3.  Sometimes the right answer is no AI at all.
4.  Reliability (guardrails, error handling, graceful degradation) is product quality.
5.  Defensible tradeoffs beat impressive-sounding complexity.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Agents are always the best/most advanced choice." Clarify that pipelines or RAG are often simpler, cheaper, and better.
•  "Architecture is an engineering-only concern." Clarify PMs must reason about it to scope and prioritize well.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is the PM track's pivot from building to judgment. PMs have now seen RAG, agents, and conversational systems; today they learn to choose among RAG, Agents, and Pipelines and to defend the tradeoffs — the single most valuable skill for the interview phase. Anchor each option to the week it was learned, and make the counter-intuitive point that agents are often not the answer. Frame reliability concepts — guardrails, error handling, graceful degradation — as product quality. This week is the seed of the entire System Design interview module (W11). Next: evaluation and optimization, the "how do we know it works and what does it cost" discipline.

Week 6.title: LLM Evaluation & Optimization
Week 6.content:
PM Module 6 (W6) — LLM Evaluation & Optimization

1. Course Journey This module gives PMs the "how do we know it works, and how do we make it better/cheaper" discipline. It exists because PMs own quality bars and must reason about evaluation, tracing, and optimization to make defensible product calls. It follows AI Product Architecture because you evaluate and optimize after you've chosen an architecture — and evaluation often reveals the architecture was wrong.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W5 — System design in agentic terms: Control (orchestrator, state management, guardrails), Execution (specialized and synthesizer agents) and Reliability (queues, isolation, memory/context).
•  W5 — AI decision-making and patterns: build vs buy for the agent stack, parallelization vs sequencing, and the reflection, tool-use, ReAct, planning and multi-agent patterns.
•  W5 — RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines: choosing the application pattern, control vs autonomy, and operational complexity.
•  W2–W4 — Building blocks: RAG and grounding, multi-agent patterns with a critic, and conversational agents with guardrails.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W5 Assignment — Multi-Agent Daily Digest (n8n): gathers multiple sources, processes each through a specialist agent and synthesizes a unified daily summary, with orchestration, guardrails, state, error handling and graceful degradation.
     Callback: ask how they would prove the digest is accurate and complete — that question is today.
•  W5 Project — Slack Project Status Chatbot (n8n): answers status, ownership, risk, priority and deadline questions in Slack from live Google Sheets data, with structured Slack-formatted responses and a dedicated error channel.
     Callback: the error channel caught failures it could see; tracing catches the wrong answers it can't.
•  W4 Project and Assignment — Product Launch Command Center and TaskFlow Product Health Monitor: multi-agent voice products with a Greeter, scoped specialists and prompt-level guardrails.
•  W3 Project and Assignment — Decision copilot and feature prioritization system (LangFlow): Planner/Analyzer/Critic workflows, with a Confidence Scorer in the copilot.
     Callback: today's tracing runs on LangFlow with Langfuse — the tool they built these in — and the Critic is an in-flow version of evaluation.
•  Earlier builds: RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent (W2); Checkout Incident Detection Agent and E-Commerce Customer Support (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: reason about LLM evaluation (metrics, tracing, human annotation); use LangFlow + Langfuse to trace and evaluate a workflow; decode traces to find failures (e.g. hallucination); and apply optimization tradeoffs. Evidenced by the ticket classification & response system — classify, assess urgency, draft, quality-check, score confidence, then find hallucinations via tracing and automated + human evaluation.

4. What this prepares learners for Evaluation is the core of the Evaluations, Safety & Governance interview module (W12) and a pillar of Production LLMOps (W13). The tracing/debugging skills feed the capstone and the System Design interview.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame evaluation as how PMs define and defend "good enough to ship."
•  Tie tracing to the debugging challenges of Week 3 orchestration.
•  Connect confidence scores and quality checks to the Critic pattern (W3).
•  Preview that Week 12 is entirely about designing evaluation systems.
•  Tie optimization back to Week 5 architecture: bad metrics may mean wrong architecture.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How do I set a quality bar for an AI feature?"
•  "Isn't LLM-as-judge circular?"
•  "What's the difference between tracing and evaluation?"
•  "How do I catch hallucinations before users do?"
•  "When is a feature 'good enough' to launch?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Evaluation operationalizes "good enough to ship."
2.  Tracing shows what happened; evaluation shows whether it was good.
3.  Human annotation and automated evals are complementary.
4.  Low metrics can indicate a wrong architecture, not just a bad prompt.
5.  Optimization is a cost/quality/latency tradeoff PMs must reason about.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Evaluation is engineering's job." Clarify PMs own the quality bar and must reason about evaluation.
•  "LLM-as-judge is unreliable." Clarify rubrics/grounding make it usable.

9. One-minute recap for instructors PMs arrive able to choose an architecture; today they learn to verify it works and optimize it — the discipline that turns opinions about quality into evidence. Keep the tracing-vs-evaluation distinction clear and address LLM-as-judge skepticism. The key PM framing is that defining "good enough to ship" is their job, expressed through metrics and golden examples. Make the link that poor metrics sometimes indict the architecture from Week 5, not just the prompt. This is the seed of the Week 12 governance interview module. Next: fine-tuning, and when it's worth it.

Week 7.title: Fine-Tuning of Agents
Week 7.content:
PM Module 7 (W7) — Fine-Tuning of Agents

1. Course Journey This module teaches PMs what fine-tuning is, what it costs, and — crucially — when it's worth it versus prompting or retrieval. It exists because "should we fine-tune?" is a recurring, expensive product decision PMs must reason about credibly. It comes last in the core curriculum because fine-tuning is the tool you reach for only after cheaper options are exhausted.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W6 — Evaluation: the hallucination problem, why PMs and TPMs must own evaluation, the tools landscape, and three approaches — agent self-evaluation, LLM-as-judge and human annotation — and how they combine.
•  W6 — Decoding traces: tokens, cost and latency in real numbers; scores, annotations and datasets; why self-evaluation failed (structure ≠ truth); and what to do when human and LLM judges disagree.
•  W6 — Optimization: four levers — prompt engineering, pipeline restructuring, model swapping and fine-tuning — the optimization loop, before-vs-after comparison, dataset-driven model comparison, and the evaluation → fine-tuning flywheel.
•  W5 — Architecture trade-offs: RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines, design patterns and reliability.
•  W2 — RAG as the knowledge lever: the fix for missing knowledge — to rule out before fine-tuning.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W6 Project — Multi-agent workflow evaluation (LangFlow + Langfuse): traced agent behavior, monitored tokens, latency and cost, scored outputs with LLM-as-judge and human annotation, measured groundedness, built evaluation datasets and ran an optimization loop.
     Callback: fine-tuning was the fourth optimization lever they met there — today is about when that lever is worth pulling.
•  W6 Assignment — Ticket classification and response system: a multi-agent workflow that classifies, assesses urgency, drafts, quality-checks and scores confidence; hallucinations on vague tickets were found through tracing, automated evals and human annotation, then reduced with prompt changes.
     Callback: prompt fixes got them part of the way — today asks what is left for fine-tuning.
•  W5 Project and Assignment — Slack Project Status Chatbot and Multi-Agent Daily Digest: architecture choices with guardrails and graceful degradation.
•  W2 Project and Assignment — RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent: their reference for "for missing knowledge, use RAG, not fine-tuning."
•  Earlier builds: Product Launch Command Center and TaskFlow Product Health Monitor (W4); decision copilot and feature prioritization system (W3); Checkout Incident Detection Agent and E-Commerce Customer Support (W1).

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: understand the fine-tuning pipeline; reason about when fine-tuning beats prompting/RAG; and evaluate its impact (e.g. reducing hallucination and improving groundedness). Evidenced by the App Review Analyzer — a multi-agent pipeline that classifies reviews and extracts insights, using DeepEval to measure groundedness before and after fine-tuning.

4. What this prepares learners for The fine-tune-vs-alternatives decision and its economics are central to Production LLMOps (W13) and appear in System Design (W11). The DeepEval before/after discipline reinforces the evaluation rigor of W12.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame as a decision: prompt vs RAG vs fine-tune, cheapest sufficient first.
•  Callback to Week 2: "for missing knowledge, use RAG, not fine-tuning."
•  Tie before/after DeepEval to Week 6 evaluation.
•  Connect to Week 5 architecture: fine-tuning is one design option, not a default.
•  Preview that Week 13 makes learners defend RAG-vs-fine-tuning live.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "When is fine-tuning worth the cost and effort?"
•  "Does fine-tuning add knowledge or change behavior?"
•  "How do I prove fine-tuning actually helped?"
•  "Can't we just prompt better or use RAG?"
•  "How do I budget for a fine-tuning project?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Fine-tuning changes behavior/style, not knowledge.
2.  Reach for it only after prompting and RAG fall short.
3.  Prove impact with before/after evaluation (DeepEval).
4.  It carries real cost and maintenance — a product tradeoff.
5.  The PM value is the decision, not the implementation.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Fine-tuning adds knowledge." Clarify: behavior vs knowledge; RAG for facts.
•  "Fine-tuning is the premium/best option." Clarify it's often unnecessary and expensive.

9. One-minute recap for instructors PMs arrive able to choose and evaluate architectures. Today they add the last decision lever — fine-tuning — and learn to reason about when it's worth it, proven with before/after evaluation. Protect the core distinction: fine-tuning changes behavior, not knowledge, so it's the wrong tool for missing facts (that's RAG). Emphasize the decision hierarchy — cheapest sufficient option first — and that the PM's value is the justified call, not the training run. This closes the core curriculum; next is the capstone, then a four-module interview-prep phase built specifically for PM/TPM roles.

Weeks 8–9.title: Project Sessions
Weeks 8–9.content:
PM Capstone (W8–9) — Project Sessions

1. Course Journey The capstone forces PMs to integrate the whole track into one system they can scope, build (in no-code), evaluate, and defend as a product decision. Options include SalesGenie, PRD Genie, Mira (project intelligence), CalendarMate, or BYOP. It sits here because PMs now hold the full toolkit plus the architecture and evaluation judgment that defines strong product work.

2. What learners already know The full track — plus a set of builds that anchor each capstone decision.
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1–W7 — The full track: reasoning agents (W1), RAG and grounding (W2), multi-agent patterns with a critic (W3), conversational and voice agents with guardrails (W4), AI Product Architecture — RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines (W5), evaluation and optimization (W6), and fine-tuning decisions (W7).
•  W7 — Fine-tuning as a gated decision: JSONL training data, when fine-tuning beats prompting or RAG, fine-tuning each agent separately, how much data is enough, handling regressions, exit criteria, and why evaluation is non-negotiable.
Prior builds each capstone option extends
•  SalesGenie — AI-Powered Sales Assistant: lead qualification, product recommendations grounded in a furniture catalog, and weekly sales reports, with observability, baseline evaluation, cost analysis and documented architecture decisions.
     Builds on: the E-Commerce Customer Support agent (W1), the RAG Intelligence Agent and AI Finance Reporting Agent (W2), and the W6 LangFlow + Langfuse evaluation workflow.
•  PRD Genie — AI-Powered Product Documentation Assistant: turns meeting transcripts, stakeholder notes and briefs into grounded PRDs, epics and prioritized user stories, flagging ambiguities; optional gap analysis, scope estimation and fine-tuning.
     Builds on: the decision copilot and feature prioritization system (W3), W2 grounding, and the W7 fine-tuning pipeline for the optional fine-tune.
•  Mira — AI-Powered Project Intelligence Assistant: project plans, risk matrices, milestone alerts and weekly status reports from project descriptions, timelines, risk registers and task boards.
     Builds on: the Slack Project Status Chatbot and Multi-Agent Daily Digest (W5), and the Risk/Reliability lens from the decision copilot (W3).
•  CalendarMate — AI-Powered Productivity Assistant: daily briefings, email summaries, meeting scheduling, conflict detection and follow-ups through calendar and email integrations.
     Builds on: the Multi-Agent Daily Digest (W5), the Zapier tool-action patterns (W1), and W5 guardrails for any action that sends or schedules.
•  BYOP: any idea — ask each learner to name the two prior builds it extends; if they can't, the scope is probably unanchored.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will: scope a product; choose and justify an architecture (RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines); build it in no-code; instrument evaluation; add guardrails; and defend cost, reliability, and UX tradeoffs. They leave with a portfolio product and a decision narrative.

4. What this prepares learners for The capstone is the concrete case the interview phase (W10–13) abstracts from — Product Sense, System Design, Governance, and Production LLMOps all reuse its decisions and metrics.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Force architecture justification against Week 5.
•  Redirect "make it fancier" toward evaluation and the right (often simpler) architecture.
•  Treat guardrails and evaluation as deliverables, not extras.
•  Frame every decision as future interview material.
•  Reward defensible restraint over feature count.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How polished/production-ready must it be?"
•  "Is BYOP riskier than a guided option?"
•  "How do I present decisions, not just a demo?"
•  "Do I need to use every technique?"
•  "How do I frame tradeoffs for an interview?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Architecture choice is the headline decision.
2.  Cheapest sufficient architecture wins.
3.  Evaluation and guardrails are deliverables.
4.  Cost, reliability, and UX tradeoffs must be explicit.
5.  The decision narrative is the product.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "More techniques = better." Clarify restraint and rationale win.
•  "The demo is the deliverable." Clarify the decisions and evaluation are.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is product integration under real constraints. PMs fuse the track into one system and, above all, defend its decisions — especially the Week 5 architecture choice. Coach relentlessly for rationale: why this architecture, what it costs, how it's evaluated, where the guardrails are, what the UX tradeoffs are. Redirect complexity instincts toward the right (often simpler) design and toward evaluation. Remind them every decision is future interview material. Reward defensible restraint. Next is the interview phase — four modules built to make them job-ready for AI PM/TPM roles.

Week 10.title: AI Product Sense & Solution Fit
Week 10.content:
PM Module 10 (W10) — AI Product Sense & Solution Fit

1. Course Journey This module converts everything learners built into product judgment they can articulate in interviews: when AI is the right solution, how to measure AI products, and how to design for trust. It exists because AI PM interviews probe solution-fit reasoning above implementation. It's first in the interview phase because product sense frames every later technical answer.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W1–W7 — The build toolkit: agents vs automation, RAG and grounding, multi-agent patterns, conversational agents and guardrails, architecture choice, evaluation and optimization, and fine-tuning decisions.
•  W5 — RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines: control vs autonomy and operational complexity — the seed of today's AI vs Non-AI 5-filter framework.
•  W6 — Evaluation: LLM-as-judge, human annotation, datasets and the optimization loop — the base for today's L0/L1/L2 metrics and counter-metrics.
•  W2, W4 — Trust patterns: response contracts users can verify, citations, safe handling of weak evidence, and voice guardrails — raw material for today's AI UX & Trust patterns (draft not done, show confidence, cite sources, graceful fallback).
Projects and assignments already built
•  Capstone (W8–9): SalesGenie, PRD Genie, Mira, CalendarMate or a BYOP product.
     Callback: their best worked example for solution-fit and "favorite AI product" answers — have them run it through the 5-filter framework.
•  W7 Project and Assignment — Fine-tuning pipeline and App Review Analyzer (n8n): DeepEval groundedness before and after fine-tuning — a ready-made metrics story.
•  W6 Assignment — Ticket classification and response system: confidence scores, quality checks and human annotation — a trust-design story.
•  W4 Project and Assignment — Product Launch Command Center and TaskFlow Product Health Monitor: voice UX and guardrails — examples for AI UX & Trust.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: navigate core interview themes (foundations, agents, knowledge, production); use a structured AI vs Non-AI decision framework; apply a metrics framework (L0/L1/L2) to AI products; reason about AI UX & Trust design; and answer from a 9-category question bank. Grounded by deep dives (a Google AI agent for working professionals; a "favorite AI product" mini-dive using Cursor).

4. What this prepares learners for Product sense frames the System Design (W11), Governance (W12), and Production LLMOps (W13) interviews. The AI-vs-non-AI framework and metrics vocabulary recur throughout.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Tie the AI-vs-non-AI framework straight to Week 5: "sometimes the answer is no AI."
•  Connect the L0/L1/L2 metrics to Week 6 evaluation.
•  Frame UX & Trust as the product face of Week 4 guardrails and Week 12 governance.
•  Use the capstone as their worked example for "favorite AI product" answers.
•  Model interview structure: framework first, then specifics.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How do I decide if a problem even needs AI in an interview?"
•  "What are L0/L1/L2 metrics and when do I use each?"
•  "How do I answer 'what's your favorite AI product'?"
•  "How technical should a PM get in a system answer?"
•  "How do I design for trust when the model can be wrong?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Product sense is structured reasoning, not opinion.
2.  The strongest answer often questions whether AI is needed at all.
3.  Metrics frameworks (L0/L1/L2) make quality legible.
4.  Trust and UX are core AI-product design problems.
5.  Frameworks first, specifics second — the interview cadence.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "AI PM interviews want deep technical detail." Clarify they reward judgment, framing, and tradeoffs.
•  "More AI is a better answer." Clarify that appropriate solution-fit — sometimes no AI — signals maturity.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This opens the interview phase by turning capability into articulable product judgment. PMs learn to decide when AI fits, to measure AI products with an L0/L1/L2 lens, and to design for trust. Anchor the AI-vs-non-AI framework to Week 5 and the metrics to Week 6, and have them rehearse "favorite AI product" using their own capstone. Model the interview cadence: framework first, specifics second. Emphasize that questioning whether AI is needed is a strength, not a dodge. The next three modules go deeper — system design, governance, and production — all framed by the product sense established here.

Week 11.title: Agentic AI System Design
Week 11.content:
PM Module 11 (W11) — Agentic AI System Design

1. Course Journey This is the direct interview extension of Week 5, teaching PMs to design agentic systems layer by layer — Knowledge, Tools/Permissions/Guardrails, Agent Architecture, Observability — and to walk an interviewer through end-to-end designs. It exists because "design an agentic system for X" is the signature AI-PM/TPM interview question. It follows Product Sense because good system design starts from solution-fit framing.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W5 — AI Product Architecture: Control, Execution and Reliability layers, design patterns, and RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines.
•  W2–W6 — Layer ingredients: chunking, metadata filtering and grounding (W2); critic loops and routers (W3); scoped knowledge bases and prompt-level guardrails (W4); state, queues, isolation and graceful degradation (W5); and tracing and evaluation with LangFlow + Langfuse (W6).
•  W10 — Product sense: the 5-filter AI vs Non-AI framework, L0/L1/L2 metrics, AI UX & Trust (visibility, verification, escape; friction calibrated to stakes), and the 9-category question bank.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W5 Assignment — Multi-Agent Daily Digest: orchestration, guardrails, state, synthesis, error handling and graceful degradation — a working example of the Agent Architecture and Tools/Guardrails layers.
•  W6 Project and Assignment — LangFlow + Langfuse evaluation and ticket classification system: tracing plus automated and human evaluation — the Observability layer in practice.
•  W2 Project — RAG Intelligence Agent: grounded, cited retrieval over enterprise documents — the Knowledge layer in practice.
•  Capstone: their own product.
     Callback: have learners describe it through the four layers before the walkthroughs begin.

3. What learners will learn today Learners will be able to: frame an agentic system-design question; reason through the Knowledge Layer, the Tools/Permissions/Guardrails Layer, the Agent Architecture Layer, and the Observability Layer, each with an interview walkthrough (YouTube Creator Policy Assistant; Google Ads Campaign Agent; AI Coding Agent; Content-Moderation Agent); and handle end-to-end questions (Consumer Fintech Money Agent; Delivery Real-Time Order Recovery).

4. What this prepares learners for The layered framework is the scaffold for the Governance (W12) and Production LLMOps (W13) interviews, which zoom into the observability/safety and production layers respectively.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Frame the four layers as the structured version of Week 5's architecture thinking.
•  Map each layer to its origin: Knowledge=W2, Tools/Guardrails=W4–W5, Architecture=W3/W5, Observability=W6.
•  Use the walkthroughs as templates for the cadence of a live answer.
•  Preview that Week 12 drills into safety/governance and Week 13 into production.
•  Stress permissions as a PM-critical, often-forgotten layer.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "In what order should I cover the layers in an interview?"
•  "How much depth per layer in 45 minutes?"
•  "How do I handle permissions and guardrails as a PM?"
•  "What makes an end-to-end answer strong vs shallow?"
•  "How do I recover if I blank mid-design?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  The four layers are a reusable design framework.
2.  Every layer needs a stated tradeoff.
3.  Permissions and guardrails are where PMs differentiate.
4.  Observability is part of the design, not an afterthought.
5.  End-to-end coherence beats depth in one layer.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "System design means naming components." Clarify it's justified tradeoffs across layers.
•  "Observability is an engineering detail." Clarify PMs must design for it to ensure quality and trust.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This is the signature AI-PM interview skill: designing an agentic system, layer by layer, out loud. It's Week 5 turned into a rehearsable framework — Knowledge, Tools/Permissions/Guardrails, Agent Architecture, Observability — with four walkthroughs as templates. Map each layer to where it was learned so it's recall, not invention, and stress the layers PMs neglect (permissions, observability). Use the end-to-end questions to practice coherence over one-layer depth. This scaffolds the final two modules, which magnify the safety/governance and production layers into full interviews.

Week 12.title: Evaluations, Safety & Governance
Week 12.content:
PM Module 12 (W12) — Evaluations, Safety & Governance

1. Course Journey This module drills the evaluation, safety, and governance reasoning that senior AI-PM interviews probe, entirely through case studies. It exists because as AI products gain autonomy, the ability to reason about what could go wrong and how you'd catch it becomes a defining PM competency. It follows System Design because governance is the layer that keeps a designed system safe in the world.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W6 — Evaluation and tracing: LLM-as-judge, human annotation, disagreement between judges, and finding hallucinations in traces.
•  W11 — Four-layer system design: Knowledge; Tools, Permissions & Guardrails (read/write/trigger gates, HITL on irreversible actions, Meta's Rule of Two); Agent Architecture (earn every extra agent, stopping conditions); Observability (health ≠ decision quality, drift, safety vs quality alerts) — with walkthroughs including an AI Coding Agent and a Content-Moderation Agent.
•  W3 — The critic instinct: a built-in checker that challenges outputs before they ship.
•  W10 — Metrics and trust: L0/L1/L2 metrics, counter-metrics, and calibrating friction to stakes.
Projects and assignments already built
•  W6 Project and Assignment — LangFlow + Langfuse evaluation and ticket classification system: automated plus human evaluation to find hallucinations — the base for "design an evaluation system."
•  W7 Project and Assignment — Fine-tuning pipeline and App Review Analyzer: DeepEval groundedness, usefulness and relevancy before and after fine-tuning — practice for metrics and thresholds.
•  W3 Project — Multi-agent decision copilot: Critic, Reviser and Confidence Scorer agents — the starting point for multi-agent reliability and arbitration.
•  W11 walkthroughs — AI Coding Agent and Content-Moderation Agent: the closest prior cases to today's safety and autonomy question (an autonomous code-deployment agent).

3. What learners will learn today Through five case-based question areas, learners will be able to: design evaluation systems (Alexa Shopping Agent); reason about metrics, thresholds & trust with audit checks (GitHub Copilot launch eval); ensure multi-agent reliability (5-Agent Travel Booking); reason about safety, autonomy & launch decisions (autonomous code-deployment agent, Devin); and debug/operate in production (customer-support agent CSAT drop). Each pairs an approach, concepts, and a case study.

4. What this prepares learners for Governance reasoning is essential for senior AI-PM roles and complements Production LLMOps (W13). The debugging case (CSAT drop) directly bridges into production operations.

5. How instructors should connect today's lesson
•  Tie evaluation-system design to Week 6 and to the Critic pattern (W3).
•  Frame safety/autonomy decisions as the product form of HITL and guardrails.
•  Connect the CSAT-drop case to Week 13's production debugging.
•  Use each case to rehearse a structured approach: define good → set thresholds → catch failures → operate.
•  Emphasize launch-decision reasoning — go/no-go under uncertainty.

6. Questions learners are likely to ask
•  "How do I design an evaluation system from scratch in an interview?"
•  "How do I set thresholds without production data?"
•  "When is an autonomous agent safe enough to launch?"
•  "How do I debug a live quality regression like a CSAT drop?"
•  "How much autonomy should an agent have?"

7. Teaching emphasis
1.  Evaluation design is a structured, teachable skill.
2.  Thresholds and audits operationalize trust.
3.  Autonomy and safety are launch-gating product decisions.
4.  Production debugging starts from metrics and traces.
5.  Case studies are rehearsal for real interview prompts.

8. Common misconceptions
•  "Safety is a compliance checkbox." Clarify it's a core design and launch decision.
•  "Evaluation is only pre-launch." Clarify production monitoring (e.g. CSAT drops) is continuous governance.

9. One-minute recap for instructors This module makes governance concrete through five real-world cases — Alexa, Copilot, a 5-agent travel booker, Devin, and a CSAT regression. PMs learn to design evaluation systems, set trust thresholds, reason about autonomy and launch safety, and debug live regressions. Run each case as a structured rehearsal: define "good," set thresholds, anticipate failures, operate. Tie it back to Week 6 evaluation and the Critic pattern, and forward to Week 13's production focus. The maturity signal to instill is treating safety and autonomy as launch-gating product decisions, not compliance. One module remains: production LLMOps.

Week 13.title: Production LLMOps Deep Dive
Week 13.content:
PM Module 13 (W13) — Production LLMOps Deep Dive

1. Course Journey The final module rehearses production reasoning — architecture, RAG-vs-fine-tuning, latency/cost, failure modes, and rollout — as senior interview questions. It exists because "how would you operate this in production" separates senior AI PMs from junior ones. It's last because it presumes all prior product, design, and governance reasoning.

2. What learners already know
Concepts and skills in hand
•  W5, W11 — Architecture choice: RAG vs Agents vs Pipelines and the four-layer system-design framework.
•  W2, W7 — RAG and fine-tuning decisions: retrieval for knowledge, fine-tuning for behavior, and the cost of each.
•  W6, W12 — Evaluation and governance: tracing, automated and human evaluation, rubric and judge calibration, launch gates, and the four-step production-debugging approach (scope → hypothesize → diagnose → close).
